$comment: Content for Respect at Home (node g56, ages 22+, Chapter 7): NEW v2 build to GDD 56 (mechanic-embodying), the
CHAPTER'S HIGHEST-SAFEGUARDING node: it carries the consent thread into marriage and committed partnership, the
place consent is most often assumed away. Marriage doesn't cancel consent, and love is never control. 84
researched, India-grounded scenarios across respect-daily → consent-inside → spot-abuse-control →
safety-and-help → never-your-fault → tools-and-help, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions
(strike-rewrite / branch / role-play / sort / reflect / spot / match): no binary "tap the right card". Lead:
strike-rewrite (bust the myth), branch (your move), role-play (say it). Five modes: respect daily (mutual
respect & an equal voice), consent inside (married is NOT standing consent; UN&RE), spot abuse & control (the
forms of domestic abuse (emotional, financial, sexual, physical) and coercive control; it's never love),
safety & help (recognising danger, safety-planning basics, where to get help, NO blame), tools/help. HIGH-STAKES
& survivor-centred throughout: NEVER victim-blaming (abuse is always the perpetrator's responsibility), urgent
disclosure routing (181, 1091, 112), even-handed across genders (men and others can be victims and are
especially silenced), strictly non-graphic. Protections framed around India's Protection of Women from Domestic
Violence Act 2005 (covering physical, emotional, sexual & economic abuse: protection orders & maintenance); the
marital-consent CRIMINAL-law landscape is contested and evolving, so this is educational, not legal advice.
Safety-planning handled with care: risk can RISE at leaving. Builds on Mutual (g31) and Consent, For Real (g44);
the protective backbone of Chapter 7 (g55 routes coercive control here). gameId "respect-at-home".
title: Respect at Home
greet: Hey, it’s Lensy. Respect doesn’t stop at the front door: marriage doesn’t cancel consent, and love is never control. Close to home? It’s never your fault.

badge.title: Respect at Home 🏠
badge.blurb: Marriage doesn’t cancel consent and love is never control; you can name abuse and coercive control; help is real. If it’s close to home, it’s not your fault. 💛

helpLine: Abuse is never the fault of the person hurt; anyone of any gender can be a victim. India’s DV Act 2005 protects you. Reach a trusted person, 181, 1091 or 112.
reassure: Close to home? Abuse is never your fault, and anyone of any gender can be hurt this way. You’re not alone. Reach a trusted person, 181, 1091 or 112. 💛

scenarios.relearn: Both opinions counting and disagreeing safely is respect; one person deciding and eggshells is its absence.
scenarios.hook: Sort: mutual respect at home, or its absence?

items.text: Each of you is heard out

scenarios.hook: Lensy: respect, an equal voice and safety belong inside the home as much as anywhere. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Respect, an equal voice and safety don't stop at your front door; they belong inside the home.
scenarios.relearn: Respect, an equal voice and safety belong inside the home as much as anywhere.

scenarios.hook: Your partner expects all the household decisions to be theirs alone.

steps.prompt: They announce a big purchase without asking you first. What do you do?

options.text: Say big decisions should be made together, starting now
options.then: They look surprised, then nod. "Fair enough," they say.

options.text: Ask them to loop you in next time, gently
options.then: They nod, but the same thing happens again a few weeks later.

options.text: Let it go, since it's already decided
options.then: The purchase stands, and the pattern continues unquestioned.

options.text: Quietly make an equally big purchase yourself
options.then: They notice the new purchase, and an argument follows about money, not decisions.

steps.why: Naming that big decisions are joint, plainly and early, claims your equal voice.

steps.prompt: A relative asks who really runs the household. What do you say?

options.text: Say you believe big calls belong to both of you
options.then: The relative raises an eyebrow, and your partner hears it said out loud.

options.text: Say your partner mostly handles the big calls
options.then: The relative nods, and the assumption quietly sticks.

options.text: Laugh and say whoever's louder that day
options.then: Everyone laughs, and the real question goes unanswered.

options.text: Say it's not really anyone's business to ask
options.then: The relative looks taken aback by the sharpness.

steps.why: Saying out loud that big decisions belong to both of you claims your equal voice in front of others.

steps.prompt: Money comes up again, this time about a family function. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll decide the budget together this time
options.then: You sit down together, and the budget gets settled jointly for once.

options.text: Suggest your partner handle it since they're good with numbers
options.then: Your partner sets it smoothly, and you're left out of the decision again.

options.text: Let them decide, like always
options.then: The budget gets set without you again, same as before.

options.text: Insist on deciding it alone this time
options.then: Your partner looks stung, and it becomes its own argument.

steps.why: Deciding the budget together turns an equal voice from an idea into a habit.

scenarios.debrief: An equal voice in decisions, money and plans is part of a respectful partnership.
scenarios.relearn: Big decisions should be made together; you have an equal voice.

scenarios.hook: "Once you're married, you give up your own rights and autonomy."

myth.un: Once married, you give up your own rights and autonomy.
myth.re: You keep your rights, autonomy and dignity inside a marriage; partnership doesn't erase them.
myth.why: A wedding ring isn't a surrender of self.

scenarios.relearn: You keep your rights, autonomy and dignity inside a marriage.
Feeling safe and having your needs taken seriously is respectful; fear and money control are warnings.
scenarios.hook: Sort: a sign of a respectful home, or a warning?

items.text: You feel safe to be yourself
Your money is controlled for you
You can speak your mind freely
You hide things to avoid a row

scenarios.hook: You want to build a home where both of you feel genuinely respected.

steps.prompt: You're planning how to run the household together. What do you do?

options.text: Make space for both voices, needs and choices from the start
options.then: You both sit down and shape it together, a little clumsily at first.

options.text: Let your partner set the rules since they're organised
options.then: The house runs smoothly, but only one voice actually shaped it.

options.text: Decide the rules alone, so it's simple
options.then: You handle it efficiently, but resentment quietly builds.

options.text: Avoid making any rules, and hope it works out
options.then: Nothing gets decided, and small frustrations pile up instead.

steps.why: Making room for both voices from the start builds the respectful home you want.

steps.prompt: A disagreement comes up about weekend plans. What do you do?

options.text: Say what you want and ask what they want too
options.then: You land on something that actually works for both of you.

options.text: Go along with their plan to avoid friction
options.then: The weekend goes fine, though it was entirely their plan again.

options.text: Insist on your own plan without asking
options.then: Your partner goes along, a little deflated.

options.text: Say what you'd like, then leave the choice to them
options.then: They choose their own plan, and your wish gets a polite nod.

steps.why: Asking what they want, alongside naming what you want, is how both voices count.

steps.prompt: Months in, life at home feels calm and busy. What do you do?

options.text: Ask each other honestly if both still feel heard
options.then: The honest answer surprises you both, in a useful way.

options.text: Assume it's fine since nothing's gone wrong
options.then: Things stay comfortable, though a few things go unsaid.

options.text: Plan a special dinner to show you care
options.then: The dinner is lovely, and neither of you mentions what's been missing.

options.text: Skip any check-in, since it would feel awkward
options.then: Small unspoken frustrations keep quietly building.

steps.why: Checking in honestly, not just assuming calm means respect, keeps a home genuinely equal.

scenarios.debrief: A respectful home actively makes room for both partners' voices, needs and choices.
scenarios.relearn: Make space for both voices, needs and choices to build a respectful home.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: in a healthy partnership, your partner is glad you have your own mind, money and friends. Recognise that?
scenarios.affirm: A good partner welcomes your independence, your mind, money and friendships; that's real respect.
scenarios.relearn: A healthy partner is glad you keep your own mind, money and friends.

scenarios.hook: "Marriage means standing, automatic consent."

myth.un: Marriage means standing, automatic consent.
myth.re: Consent is ongoing inside marriage; you can say no any time, and your body is yours.
myth.why: A relationship is not blanket permission.

scenarios.relearn: Consent is ongoing inside marriage; you can say no any time, and your body is yours.

scenarios.hook: "Forcing sex within marriage isn't really a violation."

myth.un: Forcing sex within marriage isn't really a violation.
myth.re: Coercing sex is a violation of consent and dignity, regardless of marital status or the law's current state.
myth.why: Your body remains your own inside a marriage.

scenarios.relearn: Coercing sex within marriage is a violation of consent and dignity; your body remains yours.

scenarios.hook: Your husband Vikram has started saying that marriage means you owe him sex.

steps.prompt: Tonight he says it again, as if that settles it. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him your body is yours to give, married or not
options.then: He frowns and says you've changed, but he doesn't push it tonight.

options.text: Tell yourself a good wife doesn't refuse her husband
options.then: The thought turns his words into a rule you feel you must follow.

options.text: Wonder if it's your fault for not wanting him enough
options.then: You search yourself for what's wrong, and his claim goes unquestioned.

options.text: Ask your mother what a wife is supposed to do
options.then: She says keeping him happy is part of marriage. You feel more trapped.

steps.why: Your body stays yours inside marriage. Saying so names his claim as a myth, not a rule.

steps.prompt: A few days later he jokes that you 'owe him one'. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him it isn't funny, because sex is never owed
options.then: He rolls his eyes and says you can't take a joke, then drops it for now.

options.text: Start counting your past refusals, as if he's right
options.then: You begin to feel you owe him an explanation for every no.

options.text: Tell yourself jokes like that mean he loves you
options.then: The joke starts to sound fond, and the pressure hides inside it.

options.text: Take your cousin's advice to keep him happy at any cost
options.then: She means well, but her advice makes his demand sound normal.

steps.why: A joke can still be pressure. Naming it keeps the truth clear: nothing about sex is owed.

steps.prompt: A week later he brings it up again, sounding annoyed. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a trusted friend what he keeps saying
options.then: She listens, then says clearly that it isn't owed and it isn't your fault.

options.text: Decide it's private and no one else should know
options.then: You carry it alone, and his words start to sound like the truth.

options.text: Blame yourself for being a disappointing wife
options.then: The blame lands on you, while his demand stays unquestioned.

options.text: Ask his mother whether you're being unfair to him
options.then: She says a wife should never refuse. Now the pressure comes from two sides.

steps.why: Someone you trust helps you see it clearly. His pressure is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: No one is 'owed' sex by marriage; consent is given freely every time, and pressure from a partner is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: You never 'owe' sex; consent is yours to give, always, marriage or not.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: consent doesn't expire at the wedding, it stays yours for life. Land clearly?
scenarios.affirm: Your consent is yours for life; it never expires or transfers because of a marriage.
scenarios.relearn: Consent doesn't expire at the wedding; it stays yours for life.

scenarios.hook: You want to say no to your partner without it turning into a fight.
scenarios.setup: Tonight they reach for you and you're not in the mood.

steps.prompt: They ask: "You in the mood tonight?"

options.text: "Not tonight. I'm not feeling it."
options.then: "Okay," they say, and settle in beside you instead.

options.text: "Am I even allowed to say no in a marriage?"
options.then: They pause. "I don't know. I've never thought about it."

options.text: "Why do you always ask when I'm tired?"
options.then: They frown. "That's not fair. I don't always ask."

options.text: "I suppose I owe you one after last week."
options.then: They frown at the word 'owe', and the evening turns quiet.

steps.why: A plain, calm no is easy to hear, and it needs no reason attached.

steps.prompt: They ask: "Did I do something wrong?"

options.text: "No, not at all. I'm just tired tonight."
options.then: "Fair enough," they say, relieved it isn't about them.

options.text: "You never ask at the right time."
options.then: They stiffen. "That's not what I asked you."

options.text: "I should want to. Something's wrong with me."
options.then: "Nothing's wrong with you," they say, though you don't quite believe it.

options.text: "Let's not make this a whole conversation."
options.then: They let it go, and the question stays open between you.

steps.why: An honest, simple reason reassures them without turning your no into a negotiation.

steps.prompt: The next morning they ask: "Was last night okay? I wasn't sure."

options.text: "It was. You listened, and that helped."
options.then: They smile. "Good. I want to get it right."

options.text: "Let's not talk about last night again."
options.then: They nod, unsure what to do differently next time.

options.text: "You shouldn't have to ask me that."
options.then: They look uncertain, and the door you both opened closes.

options.text: "I still feel bad about saying no."
options.then: "You don't need to," they say, though the guilt stays with you.

steps.why: Saying what worked helps a partner learn what a real yes and a real no sound like.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend Meera asks: "You seem off. Everything okay at home?"

options.text: "I said no the other night, and it left me shaky."
options.then: She listens, then says a no needs no reason and the guilt isn't yours.

options.text: "It's fine. Married people don't discuss this."
options.then: She changes the subject, and you're left with it alone.

options.text: "I think I made too much of a small thing."
options.then: She shrugs, and your own feeling gets smaller in the telling.

options.text: "Everyone says couples just work it out quietly."
options.then: She agrees easily, and nothing about it gets any clearer.

steps.why: A trusted friend can settle the guilt. Feeling pressured about a no is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: You can calmly say no to your partner; a respectful partner accepts it.

scenarios.hook: Sort each: respects consent inside a relationship, or ignores it?

items.text: Checking in and accepting a no
Waiting for a real, willing yes

scenarios.relearn: Checking in, stopping when asked, and waiting for a willing yes respect consent; pressuring, treating marriage as permission, or guilt-tripping ignore it.

scenarios.hook: You feel unsure whether you're even allowed to say no to your husband.

steps.prompt: Tonight you truly don't want to be intimate. What do you do?

options.text: Remind yourself your consent is still yours
options.then: You feel a small, steady relief just from naming it.

options.text: Assume marriage already decided this for you
options.then: The thought makes your own wishes feel like they don't count.

options.text: Tell yourself wanting to refuse makes you a bad wife
options.then: Guilt settles in, as if your feelings were the problem.

options.text: Ask your mother-in-law what a good wife would do
options.then: She says a wife doesn't refuse. You feel more unsure, not less.

steps.why: Knowing your consent stays yours is the first step, even before you say it aloud.

steps.prompt: Your husband notices you seem uneasy and asks what's wrong. What do you do?

options.text: Say gently that you don't want to tonight
options.then: He looks surprised, then nods and turns off the light.

options.text: Remind yourself it's your duty as a wife
options.then: The thought drowns out your own wish before you can find the words.

options.text: Apologise for being a difficult wife
options.then: He looks puzzled, and you end up sorry for a feeling you're allowed to have.

options.text: Ask him whether a wife is even allowed to say no
options.then: He shrugs and says he's never thought about it, leaving you to guess.

steps.why: A gentle, direct no is enough. You never have to earn it or explain it.

steps.prompt: The next day, the doubt is still with you. What do you do?

options.text: Talk it over with a friend you trust
options.then: She tells you plainly that you can always say no, and doubting it isn't your fault.

options.text: Keep the doubt to yourself, since it's private
options.then: The question stays locked inside, with no one to tell you it's okay.

options.text: Decide a wife's wishes come after her husband's
options.then: Your own wishes shrink a little more in your mind.

options.text: Take your aunt's advice to never refuse a husband
options.then: Her words echo, making your no feel like something to be ashamed of.

steps.why: Feeling unsure is never your fault. Someone you trust can help you see your right clearly.

scenarios.debrief: You are always allowed to say no inside a marriage; that right is never given up, and doubting it is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: You can always say no to your spouse; that right is never given up.

myth.why: Harm comes in many forms, not only bruises.

scenarios.hook: "What happens in a marriage is private; outsiders shouldn't be involved."

myth.un: What happens in a marriage is private; no one should get involved.
myth.re: Abuse is not a private family matter; 'private' is not a shield, and help and legal protection exist.
myth.why: Privacy must never cover for harm.

scenarios.relearn: Abuse isn't a private matter; 'private' is no shield, and help and protection exist.

scenarios.hook: You're noticing early signs of control from your husband that you'd been brushing off.

steps.prompt: He is angry you visited your sister without asking his permission. What do you do?

options.text: Name it to yourself as a controlling pattern
options.then: Naming it clearly, you start noticing how often it happens.

options.text: Tell yourself he is just having a bad week
options.then: You let it go, and the same thing comes up again days later.

options.text: Decide a wife does need approval for visits
options.then: The rule sounds normal in your head, and it spreads to other visits.

options.text: Ask his mother whether this is how it should be
options.then: She says he only worries, and you leave with the same doubt.

steps.why: Naming a pattern honestly, instead of excusing it, is how you start to see it clearly.

steps.prompt: A week later, he checks your phone messages without asking. What do you do?

options.text: Note it down, dated, somewhere he won't see
options.then: Writing it down, you see the pattern is growing, not shrinking.

options.text: Tell yourself checking is normal in a marriage
options.then: The thought settles, and the checking carries on each night.

options.text: Decide you must have given him a reason
options.then: You go back over your week looking for a fault, and find none.

options.text: Ask your cousin whether you should let him
options.then: She says a good wife has nothing to hide, and you feel worse.

steps.why: A dated note kept where he won't find it keeps the pattern visible to you while you decide what to do.

steps.prompt: At a family lunch, your sister asks quietly how things are at home. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her plainly what has been happening
options.then: She listens, then says the checking is not something you caused.

options.text: Say it is all normal in any marriage
options.then: She nods, and you carry the whole week home by yourself again.

options.text: Say what happens at home is private
options.then: She lets it drop, and the subject closes before it properly opens.

options.text: Say you will tell her once you are sure it counts
options.then: Lunch ends, and the question of whether it counts stays with you.

steps.why: Telling one trusted person what is happening is not disloyalty, and none of it is your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Early signs of control are easy to normalise; naming them honestly, and telling someone you trust, is the first protection.
scenarios.relearn: Take early signs of control seriously and name them honestly.

scenarios.hook: Since the wedding, the evenings at home have got harder to predict.

steps.prompt: Tonight the fear feels especially heavy. What do you do?

options.text: Reach out to a trusted person or a helpline like 181
options.then: A calm voice on the other end says you're not alone, and listens without judging.

options.text: Wait to see if the feeling passes on its own
options.then: The night passes, but the same fear is waiting again tomorrow.

options.text: Convince yourself you're probably overreacting a bit
options.then: You push the fear down, though it doesn't actually go away.

options.text: Ask a relative living with the family what they think
options.then: They brush it off as normal marriage stress, and you feel more alone.

steps.why: Reaching out, even to one trusted person, breaks the fear's hold before it grows.

steps.prompt: A friend notices you seem quiet and asks if you're okay. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her honestly that you're scared at home
options.then: She listens without judging, and asks what you need.

options.text: Say you're just tired from work lately
options.then: She accepts it, and the real weight stays with you alone.

options.text: Laugh it off and quickly change the subject
options.then: The moment passes, and the fear stays unspoken.

options.text: Hint at it but ask her to just drop it
options.then: She senses something is wrong but doesn't press, unsure how to help.

steps.why: Naming it honestly to someone who listens is what starts to lift the weight.

steps.prompt: The fear keeps returning most evenings. What do you do next?

options.text: Call 181 and start naming what's actually happening
options.then: They believe you straight away and walk you through what help looks like.

options.text: Decide to just get better at managing the fear alone
options.then: You cope for now, but nothing about the situation itself changes.

options.text: Blame yourself for letting things get this far
options.then: The self blame grows heavier, though none of this is your doing.

options.text: Wait for a clearer, bigger sign before doing anything
options.then: The waiting stretches on, and the fear doesn't wait with you.

steps.why: Naming it plainly to a real helpline is what finally brings real support in.

scenarios.debrief: Frightened at home? Reaching out to a helpline or trusted person is brave, and it's never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Frightened? Reach out (181, 1091, 112); you're not alone, and it's not your fault.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: abuse can escalate, especially around leaving, so safety planning matters. Important to know?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing that risk can rise around leaving, and planning for safety, is vital, careful knowledge.
scenarios.relearn: Abuse can escalate, especially around leaving; safety planning matters.

scenarios.hook: Sort: part of a safety plan, or not?

items.text: A safe place you can go
Key documents and a small bag ready
A code word with a trusted person
Telling no one and managing alone

scenarios.relearn: A safe place, key documents and a code word are part of a safety plan; confronting them alone or just hoping isn't.

scenarios.hook: Things at home have felt unpredictable, and you want to be ready just in case.

steps.prompt: You get a quiet moment alone this week. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly learn a trusted contact's number by heart
options.then: Knowing the number by heart makes you feel a little steadier.

options.text: Assume you'll figure it out if it ever comes to that
options.then: The uncertain feeling stays, unaddressed for now.

options.text: Tell yourself preparing means expecting the worst
options.then: You push the thought away, though the unease doesn't leave.

options.text: Ask a relative to keep watch without explaining why
options.then: They agree, confused, and nothing concrete actually gets planned.

steps.why: A contact you know by heart turns a vague worry into a real plan, with nothing written to be found.

steps.prompt: Later, you wonder which papers you'd need if you ever had to get somewhere safe fast. What do you do?

options.text: Keep ID copies with someone whose home you could go to
options.then: One quiet errand later, the copies wait at a door you could reach fast.

options.text: Assume you'd have time to gather papers if it came to that
options.then: The papers stay scattered around the house, where they've always been.

options.text: Decide keeping copies would be disloyal to the family
options.then: The doubt wins for now, and the papers stay in the family cupboard.

options.text: Worry over which papers matter without deciding anything
options.then: The moment passes, and nothing gets set aside.

steps.why: Papers kept at a safe place you could go to mean one less thing to find in a hurry.

steps.prompt: You think about what a code word with someone you trust could look like. What do you do?

options.text: Agree a simple code word with a trusted person
options.then: Now there's a fast, quiet way to call for help if you ever need it.

options.text: Decide you'll just explain everything in the moment
options.then: In a rushed moment, there may be no time to explain at all.

options.text: Put the idea off until things feel more urgent
options.then: The idea stays a thought, not yet something real.

options.text: Assume nobody would really understand why you're asking
options.then: You keep it to yourself, though a trusted person likely would.

steps.why: A pre-agreed code word means help can move fast, without a long explanation.

scenarios.debrief: A quiet safety plan (a trusted contact, documents, a code word, a safe place) is wise preparation. None of this is your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Quietly prepare a safety net: a trusted contact, documents, a code word, a safe place.

scenarios.hook: You've decided you need a code word with a trusted friend, just in case.
scenarios.setup: You and your friend Sana finally get a quiet moment over tea.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Everything okay? You seem like you want to say something."

options.text: "Can we agree a word I'd text you if I'm ever in trouble?"
options.then: She nods slowly. "Yes. Pick one, and I'll remember it."

options.text: "It's going to be okay, I promise. We'll figure out what to do about it together."

options.text: "What did you do to set them off?"

options.text: "Let's figure out your next move right now."

steps.prompt: Days later, over tea, she asks: "Do you think anyone else will believe me?"

options.text: "I believe you completely, and you don't have to convince anyone alone."

options.text: "I'm not sure. People can be funny about these things."

steps.why: Believing her without conditions is what makes it safe for her to keep talking.

steps.prompt: Later she says: "I don't even know where to start."

options.text: "Whenever you're ready, I can help you find a trusted number to call."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Just knowing that's there helps," she says.

options.text: "Don't worry about it too much. Things usually sort themselves out with time."

options.text: "You should call the police today."

options.text: "I'll handle it. Just leave it to me."

steps.prompt: The shame surfaces again tonight. What do you do?

options.text: Accept the shame as yours to carry

options.text: Decide you must have deserved it somehow

options.text: Believe people would judge you if they knew

steps.prompt: A friend asks gently how you're really doing. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her honestly, without the shame talking
options.then: She listens closely and says none of it was ever your fault.

options.text: Say it's old news and better left alone

options.text: Get frustrated with yourself for still feeling it

options.text: Assume healing should be finished by now

options.text: Hide it so no one sees you still struggling

options.text: "Sorry to bother you. It's probably not a big deal."

options.text: "I'm not really sure why I called."

options.text: "Can you just tell me if this counts as abuse?"

scenarios.setup: She glances at you, bracing for a reaction.

steps.prompt: She says: "I know you probably think I should just leave."

options.text: "Whatever you decide, I'm with you. No judgement, just support."
options.then: She softens. "Thank you. I really needed to hear that," she says.

options.text: "I don't think that at all. Honestly, it's not my place to say what you should do."
options.then: She looks a little relieved, but still watches your face closely.

options.text: "You have to leave right now."
options.then: She flinches. "It's not that simple," she says, pulling back.

options.text: "I don't really want to get involved in this."
options.then: She nods stiffly. "Okay, never mind then," she says.

steps.why: Support without judgement, whatever she decides, is what actually lets her keep talking.

steps.prompt: Weeks later she says she's decided to stay for now: "Please don't be disappointed in me."

options.text: "I'm not disappointed. It's your call, and none of this is your fault."
options.then: She relaxes. "That means a lot," she says.

options.text: "There's nothing to be disappointed about. You're doing the best you can right now."
options.then: She nods, but something in her posture still looks braced.

options.text: "I really think that's the wrong choice."
options.then: She stiffens. "There it is," she says, and goes quiet.

options.text: "Fine, do what you want then."
options.then: Her voice flattens. "Okay then," she says, and the topic closes.

steps.why: Saying it's her call and never her fault keeps the door open for whenever she needs you.

steps.prompt: Months later she calls, upset: "I think I'm finally ready to leave, but I'm scared."

options.text: "That's your choice to make, and I'll help however you need."
options.then: She breathes out. "Okay. Can we figure out the details together?" she asks.

options.text: "It's completely okay to be scared. Plenty of people feel exactly like this."
options.then: There's a pause on the line. "Okay, but what do I actually do?" she asks.

options.text: "Finally. I always knew you would."
options.then: Her voice tightens. "It's not really about being right," she says.

options.text: "I'll come get your things right now."
options.then: She pauses. "I need to plan this my way," she says.

steps.why: Meeting her readiness with support, not commentary, keeps the choice and the pace hers.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Can we talk about what a safe plan even looks like?"

options.text: "Yes, let's think through a safe place, documents and who to call."
options.then: Her voice steadies. "Okay, let's start with that," she says.

options.text: "Of course, we can talk through whatever feels most useful for you right now."
options.then: She agrees, though the plan itself still feels vague to her.

options.text: "Just pack a bag and go while he's out."
options.then: She hesitates. "That feels rushed," she says, uneasy.

options.text: "Let's wait until you're completely sure."
options.then: She sighs. "I don't want to just wait," she says.

steps.why: A real safety plan, thought through together, matters more than rushing or stalling.

options.text: Say you needed someone to know, for now
options.then: She says she's glad you told her, and that she isn't going anywhere.

options.text: Say you need her to promise not to judge him
options.then: She agrees, and the talk turns to protecting his name.

options.text: Say you need her to fix the whole thing
options.then: She hesitates, unsure how to take on what isn't hers to fix.

options.text: Say you need tips on keeping him calm
options.then: She offers a few, and the responsibility lands back on you.

steps.why: Saying what you actually need lets someone support you in a way that helps.

steps.prompt: Days later, you wonder whether to tell one more person. What do you do?

options.text: Decide you can tell someone else, in time
options.then: Just knowing you can feels less frightening than the first time did.

options.text: Decide that one person was already too many
options.then: The circle stays small, and so does the support around you.

options.text: Tell everyone at once to get it over with
options.then: It feels overwhelming fast, more than you were ready for.

options.text: Ask his brother to go and talk to him
options.then: He promises to handle it, and you lose your say in what happens.

steps.why: Who you tell, and when, stays your choice, at whatever pace feels safe.

scenarios.debrief: Telling a trusted person is care for yourself, never betrayal; staying quiet is never a failing, and the harm is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Telling a trusted person about harm is honesty, never betrayal, and the guilt that follows isn't yours to carry.

scenarios.hook: A man you support keeps saying he should have been 'man enough' to stop his wife's abuse.

steps.prompt: He says it again, ashamed, as you listen. What do you do?

options.text: Affirm that being harmed isn't a failure of manhood
options.then: He looks up, surprised, like it's the first time someone's said that plainly.

options.text: Agree he just needs to 'man up' about it
options.then: He nods, and the shame he came in with only sinks in deeper.

options.text: Change the subject to something less uncomfortable
options.then: He goes quiet, and the shame stays exactly where it was.

options.text: Tell him it probably wasn't that serious
options.then: He shrinks a little further, unsure now whether it's even worth mentioning.

steps.why: Affirming that harm isn't a measure of manhood names the real problem, not his character.

steps.prompt: He admits he's scared no one will believe him. What do you say?

options.text: Tell him plainly that you believe him, fully
options.then: Something in his shoulders eases, like he'd been braced for the opposite.

options.text: Say it's understandable people might doubt him
options.then: The doubt he feared feels confirmed, even gently phrased.

options.text: Suggest he wait and see how others react first
options.then: He stays guarded, unsure whether it's safe to say more.

options.text: Ask him for more proof before saying anything
options.then: He feels put on trial, and pulls back from the conversation.

steps.why: Believing him plainly, without asking for proof, is what actually makes it safe to keep talking.

steps.prompt: A few days later he asks what he should actually do next. What do you suggest?

options.text: Suggest he reach a trusted person when ready
options.then: He writes the idea down, saying he might actually try it this time.

options.text: Tell him to just handle it quietly on his own
options.then: He nods, though the isolation around it stays the same.

options.text: Tell him to confront her about it directly, alone
options.then: He looks unsure, worried about what that might make worse.

options.text: Say there's probably nothing anyone can really do
options.then: He goes quiet again, and the hope he'd started to show fades.

steps.why: Pointing toward real support respects that reaching out is his choice, made in his own time.

steps.prompt: Later, he says a friend told him men can't really be victims. What do you tell him?

options.text: Tell him that isn't true. The fault is the abuser's
options.then: He exhales, as if the words settle something in him.

options.text: Say his friend might have a point, in some ways
options.then: The doubt creeps back in, undoing some of the ground you'd covered.

options.text: Suggest he just stop talking to that friend about it
options.then: It avoids the comment, but the belief behind it stays unchallenged.

options.text: Say it's not really worth arguing about
options.then: He's left holding the friend's words with no clear answer to them.

steps.why: Saying the truth plainly, while he's hearing the myth elsewhere, is what steadies him.

scenarios.debrief: 'Man up' messaging silences male survivors; abuse is the abuser's doing, never a measure of manhood.
scenarios.relearn: Being harmed isn't a failure of manhood; the fault is the abuser's, whatever anyone's gender.

scenarios.hook: You keep thinking that if you'd stayed calmer, the violence wouldn't have escalated.

steps.prompt: The thought comes up again while you're alone. What do you do?

options.text: Recognise no tone of yours controls their violence
options.then: Saying it plainly loosens the thought's hold, at least for a moment.

options.text: Resolve never to upset them again
options.then: You take on a rule that was never actually yours to keep.

options.text: Replay the moment to find where you went wrong
options.then: The replay finds nothing solid, only more of the same searching.

options.text: Decide you must simply have a difficult temper
options.then: The thought turns inward, landing on you instead of where it belongs.

steps.why: Their violence was never something your calm could control, and it was never your fault.

steps.prompt: A counsellor asks if you've noticed yourself 'walking on eggshells'. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, and admit how tiring it's been
options.then: She nods. "That's not something you were ever meant to carry alone."

options.text: Say it's just being careful, nothing unusual
options.then: The pattern stays unnamed, even as it continues quietly.

options.text: Say you probably just need to relax more
options.then: Your own words turn the pattern back onto you, away from the one who caused it.

options.text: Deny it entirely to avoid the question
options.then: The conversation moves on, though the pattern doesn't.

steps.why: Naming the eggshell walking honestly is the first step to setting that constant vigilance down.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, you catch yourself managing your tone around someone new. What do you do?

options.text: Notice the habit and gently ask yourself why
options.then: Noticing it, without judging yourself for it, feels like real progress.

options.text: Assume it's just how you naturally are now
options.then: The habit stays invisible, carried into a relationship that doesn't need it.

options.text: Push yourself to stop the habit immediately
options.then: The pressure to fix it fast adds its own new kind of tension.

options.text: Ignore it and hope it fades with time alone
options.then: It lingers quietly, unnoticed and unaddressed.

steps.why: Noticing an old habit with curiosity, not judgement, is how it slowly starts to loosen.

scenarios.debrief: Walking on eggshells feels protective, but their violence was never yours to manage, and never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: No tone or calm of yours controls another's violence; the choice to escalate was never yours.

scenarios.hook: You're tempted to drop a complaint because people say you 'ruined his life'.

steps.prompt: A relative says it plainly at a family gathering. What do you do?

options.text: Hold that his actions changed his life
options.then: The relative falls quiet, not expecting you to hold your ground.

options.text: Believe you should be protecting his good name
options.then: You start weighing his standing in the family above your own safety.

options.text: Argue loudly to defend your decision
options.then: The argument grows heated, and the real point gets lost.

options.text: Decide the family knows best about these things
options.then: Their opinion takes over, and your own reasons fade.

steps.why: Naming where responsibility lies keeps the guilt from landing where it doesn't belong.

steps.prompt: Later, alone, you wonder whether they were right. What do you do?

options.text: Remind yourself that seeking safety ruins no one
options.then: The thought settles a little more each time you say it plainly.

options.text: Start drafting an apology to send him
options.then: Writing it feels like doing something, though it undoes what you stood for.

options.text: Ask several relatives what they honestly think
options.then: The opinions differ, and you end up less sure than before.

options.text: Decide the guilt proves you went too far
options.then: The guilt starts to look like evidence against you.

steps.why: Saying the truth to yourself matters as much as holding it in front of others.

steps.prompt: A support worker asks whether you want to carry on with the complaint. What do you say?

options.text: Ask what the next steps are, and take your time
options.then: She explains each step calmly, and nothing is decided for you.

options.text: Say your family's peace matters more than your safety
options.then: She gently asks whether that's what you believe, or what you've been told.

options.text: Say you must be selfish for starting it
options.then: She says the choice to harm was his, and the question stays yours.

options.text: Ask her to make the decision for you
options.then: She won't, and the decision waits for you anyway.

steps.why: Knowing your options, at your own pace, keeps the decision genuinely yours.

steps.prompt: Months later, someone asks how you feel about it all now. What do you say?

options.text: Say his own choices changed his life
options.then: Saying it out loud feels steadier than it used to.

options.text: Say some things are better kept inside a family
options.then: The old rule speaks again, though it changes nothing about what he did.

options.text: Say you feel guilty for what happened to him
options.then: The guilt lands on you, and his choices slip out of view.

options.text: Say the family still hasn't forgiven you
options.then: Their disapproval speaks louder than your own reasons.

steps.why: His choices, not your complaint, changed his life, and none of it was ever your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Abusers often flip blame onto the survivor; the consequences flow from his actions, and none of it is your fault.
scenarios.relearn: His actions, not your complaint, changed his life; seeking safety never 'ruins' the abuser.

scenarios.hook: You believe the abuse must be a punishment you somehow earned.

steps.prompt: The belief surfaces again on a hard day. What do you do?

options.text: Reject the idea that anyone earns abuse
options.then: Saying it firmly quiets the belief for a moment.

options.text: Search your past for what you must have done
options.then: The search turns up nothing solid, only more uncertainty.

options.text: Decide you're simply unlucky, and leave it there
options.then: It softens the belief without naming who was responsible.

options.text: Believe the harm must have been a lesson for you
options.then: The belief dresses the harm up as something you needed.

steps.why: Rejecting the idea of deserving it loosens its grip. No one ever earns abuse.

steps.prompt: At a counselling session the belief comes up, and she asks what it tells you. What do you say?

options.text: Describe it plainly, in the words it uses
options.then: She listens, then says the voice is old, and it still isn't true.

options.text: Say it's just common sense. That's how life works
options.then: She gently pushes back, and the belief stays lightly questioned.

options.text: Say everyone probably deserves what happens to them
options.then: She hears a larger belief underneath, worth returning to.

options.text: Say it must be true, since it has lasted so long
options.then: Its age starts to feel like proof.

steps.why: Describing the belief out loud lets someone else say plainly that it was never your fault.

steps.prompt: Months later, the belief still comes, though not every day. What do you do?

options.text: Let it be quieter without demanding it vanish
options.then: The quieter version feels like real, if partial, progress.

options.text: Get frustrated that it hasn't fully left yet
options.then: The frustration adds new weight to something already heavy.

options.text: Assume its quiet means you were wrong to question it
options.then: The old belief creeps back in through the doubt.

options.text: Decide you'll only be healed once it's gone
options.then: Healing turns into a test you seem to keep failing.

steps.why: Letting a belief grow quieter, without needing it gone, is honest, steady progress.

scenarios.debrief: The belief that abuse is 'deserved' is the abuser's lie taking root; nothing you are makes harm just, and it was never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: No one earns or deserves abuse; it's the abuser's choice, never a punishment you brought on yourself.

scenarios.hook: You worry that asking for help will prove you 'couldn't handle' your own marriage.

steps.prompt: You're about to reach out, then hesitate. What do you do?

options.text: See reaching out as strength, not a personal failure
options.then: Naming it that way makes the next step feel possible.

options.text: Believe a good wife handles her home alone
options.then: The rule takes the phone right out of your hand.

options.text: Decide your trouble isn't serious enough for help
options.then: The bar keeps rising, and help stays for other people.

options.text: Believe help is only for people ready to leave
options.then: Help starts to look like a step you aren't ready for, so you hold back.

steps.why: Seeing reaching out as strength is what lets you take the first real step.

steps.prompt: The next day, a trusted relative calls while you're alone and asks how you are. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her honestly, as much as feels safe
options.then: She listens without judging, and stays on the line a long while.

options.text: Say you're managing, as a wife should
options.then: She takes it at face value, and the real reason stays unsaid.

options.text: Say you shouldn't be bothering anyone with this
options.then: She reassures you, though the doubt stays close to the surface.

options.text: Ask about her life instead of your own
options.then: The conversation drifts, and what you needed goes unsaid.

steps.why: The truth, even in parts, is what lets someone help. None of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, you think about how long you've carried this alone. What do you do?

options.text: Remind yourself no one should carry this alone
options.then: The thought sits more comfortably than any blame would.

options.text: Blame yourself for waiting as long as you have
options.then: The blame adds itself to everything else you're carrying.

options.text: Decide it's too late for help to matter now
options.then: The thought discourages a next step, when one might still help.

options.text: Compare your timing to how others managed
options.then: The comparison leaves you behind, on a timeline that was never fair.

steps.why: No one should face this alone, and asking, whenever it happens, is never too late.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, your friend Lata seems to be struggling quietly too. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're there if she ever wants to talk
options.then: She looks at you a long moment, then says she may take you up on it.

options.text: Say nothing, since it isn't really your place
options.then: She stays quiet too, and nothing about her week changes.

options.text: Tell her to try managing it herself first
options.then: It hands her the same hesitation that kept you silent.

options.text: Assume she'll ask if she really needs to
options.then: She doesn't ask, and carries it the way you once did.

steps.why: Being there, at her pace, makes asking for help feel possible for her too.

scenarios.debrief: Abuse isn't a problem you were meant to solve alone; asking for help is courage, and none of it is your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Reaching out for help is strength, not failure; no one should face abuse alone, and it isn't your fault.

scenarios.hook: You feel responsible because you introduced your abuser to your family and friends.

steps.prompt: The thought surfaces while you're with your family. What do you do?

options.text: Remember you couldn't have known his choices
options.then: The guilt eases slightly. His choices were never yours to predict.

options.text: Carry the guilt of having 'brought him in'
options.then: The guilt sits heavily, attached to a decision made in good faith.

options.text: Tell yourself your family will never trust you again
options.then: The fear piles onto the guilt, and his choices drop out of view.

options.text: Apologise to your family for introducing him
options.then: They reassure you, though the apology suggests a fault that isn't really yours.

steps.why: You couldn't have known his choices. They were his alone, and never your fault.

steps.prompt: A family member says gently: "We liked him too, at first." What do you say?

options.text: Say that's exactly why none of you knew
options.then: She nods slowly, relief crossing her face too.

options.text: Say you should have seen through him sooner
options.then: She disagrees, but the thought stays with you regardless.

options.text: Say you all should have been more careful
options.then: The comment spreads a quiet blame across the whole family.

options.text: Change the subject to avoid it entirely
options.then: The moment passes, and the shared relief goes unspoken.

steps.why: Naming that no one could have known, together, lifts the guilt off you and off them too.

steps.prompt: Later, alone, the guilt about introducing him comes back. What do you do?

options.text: Talk to a friend you trust about the guilt
options.then: She listens, then says his choices were his alone, and none of it is on you.

options.text: Decide you'll never fully trust anyone again
options.then: The guardedness protects you, though it also keeps closeness at a distance.

options.text: Take a relative's advice to never speak of him again
options.then: The silence keeps the guilt hidden, and untouched.

options.text: Decide your instincts can't be trusted anymore
options.then: Every new person starts to feel like a test you'll fail.

steps.why: Someone you trust can say it plainly: his choices were his, and never your fault.

steps.prompt: Months later, a new friend seems kind and easy to trust. What do you do?

options.text: Let yourself get to know them, at a pace that feels right
options.then: Over a few weeks, you learn who they are, and the friendship grows.

options.text: Hold back completely until they prove themselves fully
options.then: The distance keeps you safe, though it also keeps you lonely.

options.text: Trust them quickly, to prove that you still can
options.then: It feels easy for now, though it's driven by something to prove.

options.text: Ask your family to vet them first
options.then: They agree, relieved, and your own judgement takes a back seat.

steps.why: Trusting at your own steady pace honours both the caution and the connection.

scenarios.debrief: You trusted in good faith; an abuser's later choices are his, not a verdict on your judgement.
scenarios.relearn: Trusting someone who later abused isn't your fault; his choices were always his own.

scenarios.hook: You assume that because you're a man, no one will treat your abuse as real.

steps.prompt: You sit with the phone, a helpline number already typed in. What do you do?

options.text: Remind yourself help is for survivors of any gender
options.then: The thought loosens the certainty that you'd be laughed at.

options.text: Believe men are never taken seriously in this
options.then: The belief keeps your thumb hovering over the screen.

options.text: Decide it only counts if there are marks to show
options.then: The rule leaves out most of what has been happening at home.

options.text: Ask a friend if it's worth making a fuss
options.then: He jokes about it, and the doubt digs itself in deeper.

steps.why: Support exists for survivors of every gender, whatever anyone assumes.

steps.prompt: That evening, the number is still on your screen. What do you do?

options.text: Call the number and say plainly what's happening
options.then: The voice on the line listens without a joke and asks what you need.

options.text: Close the screen and search for stories like yours
options.then: The stories feel familiar, but no one hears yours.

options.text: Decide a man should sort this out himself
options.then: You're back where you started, carrying it alone.

options.text: Wait until you have proof to show someone
options.then: Collecting proof becomes the task, and the weight stays yours.

steps.why: Saying it plainly to someone who can help lets them respond to what's really happening.

steps.prompt: The next day, a friend asks why you've been so quiet. What do you say?

options.text: Tell him honestly what's happening at home
options.then: He takes it seriously, and says none of it is on you.

options.text: Say it was nothing worth repeating
options.then: The moment closes, and the honesty stays unshared.

options.text: Say your marriage is nobody else's business
options.then: He backs off, and you keep carrying it alone.

options.text: Joke that your wife keeps you in line
options.then: He laughs, and the joke covers something that matters.

steps.why: Telling a friend honestly keeps you from carrying it alone. It was never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Male and other silenced survivors deserve help; the routes belong to you too, and none of it is your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Survivors of any gender deserve help; reach a trusted person, free legal aid on 15100, or 112 in danger; it's never your fault.

scenarios.hook: You feel you can't grieve the relationship because 'you chose him'.

steps.prompt: A wave of grief catches you off guard. What do you do?

options.text: Let yourself grieve without blaming your past choice
options.then: The grief comes fully for a moment, without the extra weight of blame.

options.text: Decide the grief is a punishment you signed up for
options.then: The grief turns into a sentence instead of a feeling.

options.text: Hide the grief so no one says 'you chose him'
options.then: The grief goes underground, where no one can comfort it.

options.text: Take a cousin's advice to just move on quickly
options.then: Moving on becomes the task, and the grief waits underneath.

steps.why: Grieving without blaming your past choice lets the feeling move. It was never your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later, a close friend notices you seem low and asks how you really are. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her honestly that you're grieving him
options.then: She listens, and says you don't have to justify missing what you hoped for.

options.text: Say you have no right to grieve, since you chose him
options.then: She gently disagrees, though the feeling stays with you a while longer.

options.text: Tell her, then spend the evening defending your choice
options.then: The talk becomes a defence of a choice that never needed one.

options.text: Say you're fine and change the subject
options.then: The grief waits, unexpressed, for another moment to surface.

steps.why: Saying it honestly, without defending your choice, lets someone actually be there with you in it.

steps.prompt: Months later, you notice the grief has changed shape but is still there sometimes. What do you do?

options.text: Let it be part of healing, without a strict timeline
options.then: Some days it barely shows, and some days it still does, and both feel okay now.

options.text: Push yourself to be fully done grieving by now
options.then: The pressure adds tension to a process that was never on a fixed schedule.

options.text: Assume its return means you haven't really healed
options.then: The return gets misread as failure, instead of as something grief simply does.

options.text: Decide the grief proves you still love him
options.then: The thought makes feeling anything at all seem dangerous.

steps.why: Letting grief keep its own timeline, without judging its return, is part of healing honestly.

scenarios.debrief: Loving someone who later abused you was never a mistake to be punished for; the harm was not your fault, and grief is yours.
scenarios.relearn: Loving someone who turned abusive isn't a fault; you're allowed to grieve and to heal without blame.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that wrongly put the blame on the survivor.

scene.text: "The only one responsible is the one who hurt you."
"You must have done something to set him off."
"I believe you, and none of this is your fault."
"If you'd kept quiet, it wouldn't have happened."
"What he chose to do is on him, not you."

scenarios.why: 'You must have done something' and 'if you'd kept quiet' shift blame to the survivor; the others don't.
scenarios.relearn: 'You must have done something' and 'if you'd kept quiet' are false; the fault is the abuser's.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths that excuse the abuser by blaming something else.

scene.text: "It was the drink talking, not really him."
"He chose to raise his hand; that's on him."
"His temper is his to manage, not yours."
"His rough childhood means you can't blame him."
"Plenty of stressed people never abuse anyone."

scenarios.why: 'The drink talking' and 'his rough childhood' both excuse the abuser; the rest keep responsibility with him.
scenarios.relearn: Alcohol or a hard past may explain context, but never excuse abuse; the choice stays the abuser's.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that wrongly suggest a man can't be a real victim.

scene.text: "Anyone of any gender can be abused."
"A real man would have just hit back."
"You're believed, and it's not your fault."
"Men can't really be victims of this."
"Male survivors deserve help and support."

scenarios.why: 'A real man would hit back' and 'men can't be victims' deny male survivors; the others affirm them.
scenarios.relearn: Anyone of any gender can be abused; 'real men hit back' and 'men can't be victims' are false and silencing.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that blame a survivor for staying.

scene.text: "Leaving is hard and risky; staying isn't your fault."
"If it were really that bad, you'd have left."
"You stayed for good reasons; none of this is on you."
"You chose to stay, so you can't complain now."
"Whatever you decide, the abuse was still his doing."

scenarios.why: 'You'd have left' and 'you chose to stay, so you can't complain' blame staying; the others don't.
scenarios.relearn: Staying is never a reason for blame; leaving is hard, and the abuse stays the abuser's doing.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two responses that load shame onto the survivor.

scene.text: "The shame belongs to him, never to you."
"You've brought shame on the whole family."
"Telling me took courage; I'm glad you did."
"Keep it quiet, people will think badly of you."
"None of this reflects on your worth."

scenarios.why: 'You've brought shame on the family' and 'keep it quiet' load shame onto the survivor; the rest lift it.
scenarios.relearn: Shame belongs to the abuser, not the survivor; 'you shamed the family' and 'keep quiet' are wrong.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two reactions that interrogate a survivor instead of believing them.

scene.text: "I believe you. What do you need right now?"
"Are you sure you're not exaggerating?"
"This isn't your fault, and I'm here."
"What did you do to provoke it, exactly?"
"Take your time; I'm listening."

scenarios.why: 'Are you sure you're not exaggerating?' and 'what did you do to provoke it?' interrogate and blame; the rest believe.
scenarios.relearn: Believe first; interrogating ('are you sure?', 'what did you do?') doubts and blames a survivor.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two beliefs that wrongly tie abuse to who the survivor is.

scene.text: "Abuse reflects the abuser, not your worth."
"This keeps happening, so it must be you."
"Some people simply choose to harm."
"You attract this because of who you are."
"What was done to you is on them, not you."

scenarios.why: 'It must be you' and 'you attract this' blame the survivor's character; the rest place fault on the abuser.
scenarios.relearn: Abuse reflects the abuser's choices, not your character; 'it must be you' and 'you attract it' are false.

scenarios.hook: Sort each line: does it free a survivor of blame, or load blame onto them?

items.text: "The only one responsible is the one who hurt you."
"It's never your fault, whatever you did."
"If you'd been a better wife, this wouldn't happen."
"What he chose is on him, not on you."
"You stayed, so you brought it on yourself."

scenarios.relearn: Lines placing fault on the abuser free a survivor; 'you provoked it', 'better wife', 'you stayed' blame.

scenarios.hook: Sort: where does responsibility for the abuse truly lie?

items.text: What the survivor wore that day
The survivor saying no to sex
The abuser ignoring a clear no
The survivor being tired or upset

scenarios.relearn: Responsibility lies in the abuser's choices to harm, control or ignore a no; never in what a survivor wore, said or felt.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a supportive response to a survivor, or a blaming one?

items.text: "I believe you, and it's not your fault."
"What did you do to set him off?"
"You're safe to tell me, take your time."

scenarios.relearn: Belief, safety and 'what do you need?' support a survivor; 'what did you do?' and 'kept quiet?' blame them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a true statement about fault, or a harmful myth?

items.text: Abuse is never the victim's fault
Anyone of any gender can be a victim
Staying means it wasn't really abuse

scenarios.relearn: It's never the victim's fault and anyone can be a victim; 'provocation causes it', 'men can't', 'staying' are myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a myth that blames the survivor, or a truth that clears them?

items.text: The choice to harm was his alone
Leaving is hard and risky, not a fault

scenarios.relearn: 'You provoked him', 'you shamed us', 'should have left' are blaming myths; the abuser's choice and the survivor's clearing are the truth.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a step that releases self-blame, or a trap that keeps it?

items.text: Naming that only the abuser chose to harm
Letting a trusted person remind you it's not your fault

scenarios.source: asking a friend to be your contact
scenarios.hook: You've decided you want one trusted friend ready to act fast, just in case.
scenarios.setup: Over coffee with your friend Neha, your cup sits untouched.

steps.prompt: She asks: "You've gone quiet. What's on your mind?"

options.text: "Can you be the person I call if I'm ever in danger? I may need you fast."
options.then: She sets down her cup. "Yes. Of course I will."

options.text: "Nothing really. I'm just tired today."
options.then: She studies you. "Okay. But I'm here if it's more than tired."

options.text: "I've just been thinking about safety lately, in general."
options.then: She leans in. "If something's worrying you, I want to know."

options.text: "If things ever get really bad, I'll tell you. Don't worry."
options.then: She frowns. "Why wait for really bad? I'm right here now."

steps.why: Asking plainly is what turns a vague worry into a real request she can say yes to.

steps.prompt: She waits, then says: "If you're ever in trouble, tell me exactly what to do."

options.text: "If I call and can't talk, ring 112 and send help to me."
options.then: "Got it," she says. "I'll keep my phone on me, always."

options.text: "Just be available if I ever text you sometime."
options.then: She nods. "Always. I just hope I'd know what you need."

options.text: "Nothing. I don't want to drag you into my troubles."
options.then: She shakes her head. "You're not dragging me anywhere."

options.text: "Maybe just check on me every so often."
options.then: She smiles. "I can do that. I'll message on Sundays."

steps.why: A clear, safe instruction lets her get help to you fast without walking into danger herself.

steps.prompt: A week later, she asks: "Has anything changed since we talked?"

options.text: "No, but knowing I can call you still helps a lot."
options.then: "Good," she says. "I'm not going anywhere."

options.text: "Not really. Let's not talk about it again."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. I'll still check in now and then."

options.text: "I probably won't ever actually need you."
options.then: "Maybe not," she says, "but I'm here if you do."

options.text: "Maybe this should stay inside the family after all."
options.then: She frowns. "I'm not family, but I still want to know you're safe."

steps.why: Saying it still helps keeps the plan real, and needing it was never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Ask a trusted friend to be your emergency contact, and say clearly what you need.

scenarios.hook: You've finally come to see a counsellor, after weeks of putting it off.
scenarios.setup: The clock on her desk ticks louder than it should.

steps.prompt: She says: "Take your time. What brings you in today?"

options.text: "I'm being controlled and hurt at home, and I want help."
options.then: She nods gently. "Thank you for telling me. Let's talk through it."

options.text: "I've just been feeling stressed lately, mostly."
options.then: "Okay," she says. "Tell me more about that stress."

options.text: "I'm not sure this is even worth your time."
options.then: "It is," she says warmly. "Whatever brought you here matters."

options.text: "Can we talk about something lighter first?"
options.then: "Of course," she says, "whenever you're ready for the rest."

steps.why: Naming it plainly, right away, is what lets real support begin.

steps.prompt: She asks: "What's an ordinary week at home like for you?"

options.text: "He decides the money, and watches who I talk to."
options.then: "That's coercive control," she says. "It's not okay, and it's not your fault."

options.text: "It's hard to put into words, honestly."
options.then: "That's okay," she says. "We can take it one piece at a time."

options.text: "Maybe I'm just being too sensitive about it."
options.then: "You're not," she says gently. "Whatever you feel is worth hearing."

options.text: "It's just normal marriage stuff. Private, really."
options.then: "Private doesn't mean you carry it alone," she says.

steps.why: Naming the specifics lets her name it back as coercive control, and say the fault is never yours.

steps.prompt: She asks: "What would you like support to look like, going forward?"

options.text: "Understanding my options, without being pushed into any."
options.then: "That's exactly how we'll do this," she says. "Your pace, your choice."

options.text: "Just tell me what most people in my situation do."
options.then: "I can share that," she says, "but your situation is your own."

options.text: "I want you to tell me what to do."
options.then: "I can't decide for you," she says kindly, "but I'll help you think it through."

options.text: "I don't really know what I want yet."
options.then: "That's okay too," she says. "We can figure it out together."

steps.why: Asking for options without pressure is what keeps every choice genuinely yours.

steps.prompt: Before you leave, she asks: "Is there anything you'd like to take away today?"

options.text: "A number I can call if it gets worse at home."
options.then: "181," she says. "It's short, so there's nothing to write down."

options.text: "Nothing for now. I'll see how the week goes."
options.then: "That's alright," she says. "The door stays open."

options.text: "Just tell me this will get better on its own."
options.then: "I can't promise that," she says gently, "but you're not alone in it."

options.text: "Maybe something I can show my husband."
options.then: She pauses. "Let's think first about what would be safe for you."

steps.why: Leaving with a number you can actually call turns one session into a route you can use.

scenarios.relearn: Naming 'I'm being hurt at home and I want help' to a counsellor is enough to start.

scenarios.source: what to say to a survivor
scenarios.hook: A friend has just told you, quietly, that she's being abused at home.
scenarios.setup: The first words you say next will matter.

steps.prompt: She says: "I don't even know why I'm telling you this."

options.text: "I believe you. This isn't your fault. I'm here. What do you need?"
options.then: She lets out a breath. "I needed to hear that," she says quietly.

options.text: "It's going to be okay. I promise you that."
options.then: She nods. "Maybe," she says, though the self blame doesn't fully lift.

options.text: "What did you do to set them off?"
options.then: She goes quiet, turning the question over in her head.

options.text: "Let's sit down and figure out your next move together, right now."
options.then: She nods slowly, but still looks braced, like the blame hasn't lifted.

steps.why: Naming belief, no fault and presence together is what steadies her most.

steps.prompt: She says: "I keep wondering if I somehow caused this."

options.text: "You didn't. The only person responsible is the one hurting you."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "Thank you. I keep forgetting that," she says.

options.text: "Try not to think about it that way too much."
options.then: She nods, though the thought clearly hasn't loosened its grip.

options.text: "Well, what were things like right before it happened, exactly?"
options.then: She tenses, feeling like she's being asked to explain herself.

options.text: "These things happen. It's nobody's fault really."
options.then: She frowns slightly. "It feels like it's supposed to be someone's."

steps.why: Naming the abuser as responsible is what actually answers her self blame.

steps.prompt: Days later, she messages: "Do you think anyone else will believe me?"

options.text: "I believe you, and you don't owe anyone proof to deserve help."
options.then: She relaxes a little. "Okay. That helps," she says.

options.text: "Of course they will. Don't even worry about it."
options.then: She goes quiet. "You can't really promise that," she says.

options.text: "People might ask a lot of questions, so you'd better be ready."
options.then: She tenses up. "So now I have to defend myself," she says.

options.text: "I'm not sure. People can be funny about these things."
options.then: She sighs. "That's what I was afraid of," she says.

steps.why: Believing her without conditions is what makes it safe for her to keep talking.

steps.prompt: Later she says: "I don't even know where to start."

options.text: "Whenever you're ready, we can call 181 together."
options.then: She breathes out. "Together. Okay, I can think about that."

options.text: "Don't worry about it too much. It usually sorts itself out."
options.then: She looks away. "I don't think it will," she says quietly.

options.text: "You should call the police today."
options.then: She stiffens. "I'm not ready for that yet," she says.

options.text: "I'll handle it. Just leave it to me."
options.then: She frowns. "I want to decide that myself," she says.

steps.why: Offering a route at her pace respects that the next step is hers to choose.

steps.prompt: Weeks later she says: "I've been thinking about what you said."

options.text: "Whatever you've decided, I'm with you. What do you need?"
options.then: She smiles. "Just knowing that helps," she says.

options.text: "Good. So are you finally going to do something?"
options.then: She stiffens. "There it is," she says quietly.

options.text: "I've been waiting for you to come round."
options.then: She looks stung. "It wasn't about coming round," she says.

options.text: "Let's not get heavy today. Tell me something happy instead."
options.then: She hesitates. "Okay," she says, and keeps the rest to herself.

steps.why: Backing whatever she's decided, and asking what she needs, honours the pace she set.

scenarios.relearn: To a survivor say: I believe you. It's not your fault. I'm here. Believe first, never interrogate.

scenarios.hook: You've dialled 181, and your heart is pounding as it starts to ring.
scenarios.setup: Someone picks up, calm and steady.

steps.prompt: She says: "Women Helpline, I'm listening. Go ahead whenever you're ready."

options.text: "I'm being hurt at home and I need help."
options.then: "Thank you for telling me," she says. "You're not alone in this."

options.text: "Sorry, is this even the right number to call?"
options.then: "It is," she says warmly. "Tell me what's going on."

options.text: "I don't know if this really counts as an emergency."
options.then: "You don't need it to be an emergency to call," she says gently.

options.text: "Can I just ask a few questions first?"
options.then: "Of course," she says. "Ask me anything you need to."

steps.why: Saying it plainly is enough. You don't have to justify the call, and none of it is your fault.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Are you safe to talk right now?"

options.text: "For now. If I go quiet, someone's come in."
options.then: "Understood," she says. "Then let's start. Tell me what's happening."

options.text: "Does it matter? I'm probably wasting your time."
options.then: "It matters," she says. "And you're not wasting anything."

options.text: "Not really, but I'll talk anyway."
options.then: "Your safety comes first," she says. "Talk only if you can stay safe."

options.text: "Is it even okay to talk about my husband like this?"
options.then: "It is," she says gently. "What happens at home still matters."

steps.why: Saying you can talk, and what silence would mean, lets her help and keep you safe.

steps.prompt: Before ending the call, she asks: "Is there anything specific you'd like to know?"

options.text: "What I can actually do next, step by step."
options.then: She walks you through a few clear, calm options, one at a time.

options.text: "Just tell me if I'm overreacting or not."
options.then: "You're not," she says. "But let's focus on what helps you now."

options.text: "I'm not sure, maybe nothing for now."
options.then: "That's alright," she says. "This number is here whenever you are."

options.text: "Can you just tell me what to do?"
options.then: "The choice stays yours," she says kindly, "but I'll explain the options."

steps.why: Asking what comes next, plainly, turns a nervous call into real guidance.

scenarios.relearn: On 181, 'I'm being hurt at home and I need help' is enough; they guide you from there.

scenarios.hook: You've decided to ask a trusted relative to hold onto some copies for you.
