steps.prompt: She says: "You look like you want to ask me something."

options.text: "Could you keep copies of my important papers safe, just in case?"
options.then: She looks at you steadily. "Of course. Bring them whenever you're ready."

options.text: "Could you just hold onto a few things for me sometime?"
options.then: She agrees, though she's unsure exactly what you mean.

options.text: "Never mind. It's probably not that important."
options.then: She pauses. "Okay. But you can ask me anything, any time."

options.text: "Can you keep a secret for me, no questions asked?"
options.then: She hesitates. "That depends what kind of secret," she says.

steps.why: Naming exactly what you're asking for is what makes it easy for her to say yes.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Is everything alright? You seem a bit on edge."

options.text: "I'm being careful, just in case. I'd rather not say more."
options.then: "Okay," she says. "I won't ask more. I'm just glad to help."

options.text: "Amma says family troubles should stay in the family."
options.then: She frowns. "Not when you're this worried, they shouldn't."

options.text: "Everything's completely fine. Don't worry about it."
options.then: She seems unconvinced, but doesn't push further.

options.text: "I'll tell you everything some other time."
options.then: She agrees, though the moment leaves her a little uneasy.

steps.why: An honest, calm answer keeps the ask simple, and needing to prepare is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later, she says: "I keep thinking about our talk. How can I help?"

options.text: "Keep my papers and a little money safe, if that's alright."
options.then: "Of course," she says. "It's all safe here whenever you need it."

options.text: "Maybe just my papers. The money is fine at home for now."
options.then: "Alright," she says. "Just say if you change your mind."

options.text: "I'm not sure. Maybe I'm overdoing this."
options.then: "There's no such thing," she says gently. "Better ready than not."

options.text: "Actually, let's forget the whole thing."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Alright. But the offer stays open."

steps.why: Keeping papers and a little money with someone you trust builds real readiness.

scenarios.relearn: Ask a trusted person to safely hold copies of your key documents, so you can leave fast if you choose.

scenarios.source: a quiet word with a neighbour
scenarios.hook: Things at home have got harder, and your neighbour Meena is the only person you see alone.
scenarios.setup: She catches you at the gate one evening.

steps.prompt: Meena asks quietly: "Is everything alright at home?"

options.text: "Things aren't okay. Could we talk when no one's around?"
options.then: Meena nods. "Of course. Tomorrow morning, my kitchen."

options.text: "It's a private family matter."
options.then: Meena steps back. "I'm home most days," she says, still watching you.

options.text: "My mother in law says home things stay at home."
options.then: Meena says softly: "She isn't the one carrying it, though."

options.text: "Nothing a bit more patience won't fix."
options.then: Meena looks unconvinced. "Patience shouldn't cost you this much."

steps.why: Naming it quietly and asking for a private moment turns a caring glance into real help.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Meena says: "I'm here for you. Is there anyone else you trust?"

options.text: "Not really. Could you tell me how 181 works?"
options.then: Meena explains softly. "You can call anytime, even just to ask questions."

options.text: "Only family should know about family things."
options.then: Meena shakes her head. "Some help comes from outside the family."

options.text: "No one. I should be able to manage alone."
options.then: Meena sits with you a while. "Managing alone isn't the same as being safe."

options.text: "My aunt says a helpline only brings trouble."
options.then: Meena frowns. "Asking a question brings no trouble to anyone."

steps.why: Asking about a route like 181 builds support beyond one neighbour. None of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: Meena asks: "What would help most right now, without anyone finding out?"

options.text: "Keep checking on me, and note today's date."
options.then: Meena writes it in her diary. "I'm here. Come to me anytime."

options.text: "Nothing. I probably bring some of it on myself."
options.then: Meena shakes her head. "Nobody brings this on themselves." You part with no plan made.

options.text: "Tell me what you would do in my place."
options.then: Meena hesitates. "It's your life. I don't want to decide it for you."

options.text: "Talk to my husband. He listens to neighbours."
options.then: Meena looks alarmed. "That could land straight back on you."

steps.why: A quiet, specific ask for a dated note and a regular check keeps you safer without any alarm.

scenarios.relearn: A quiet 'things aren't okay. Can we talk in private?' to a trusted neighbour is a safe first step.

steps.prompt: Karan asks: "You've seemed off for weeks now. What's going on?"

options.text: "I'm being abused at home, and I need support."
options.then: Karan sits up. "I believe you. Tell me what you need."

options.text: "Nothing a man should be complaining about."
options.then: Karan frowns. "Says who? I'm asking as your friend."

options.text: "It's on me. I'm not easy to live with."
options.then: Karan shakes his head. "That doesn't sound like the whole story."

options.text: "My uncle says home trouble stays indoors."
options.then: Karan puts his cup down. "Your uncle isn't the one living it."

steps.why: Naming it plainly, even briefly, lets a friend actually hear you and help.

steps.prompt: A week later, Karan asks: "How are things now? I've been worrying about you."

options.text: "Bad enough that I need help. I'm not imagining it."
options.then: Karan nods slowly. "Then we find you some help."

options.text: "Not bad. Men are meant to handle this quietly."
options.then: Karan says: "Nobody is meant to handle being hurt."

options.text: "It only gets bad when I get something wrong."
options.then: Karan says quietly: "That isn't how being hurt works."

options.text: "Keep it between us. My family would laugh."
options.then: Karan nods. "It stays between us. But keep talking to me."

steps.why: None of this is your fault, and saying plainly that you need help is what lets a friend act.

steps.prompt: Karan asks: "Would it help to talk to someone trained for this?"

options.text: "Yes. Will you sit with me while I find a counsellor?"
options.then: Karan opens his phone. "We'll look together this evening."

options.text: "Those services are only for women, surely."
options.then: Karan says: "A counsellor will hear you. So will 112 if it turns dangerous."

options.text: "My cousin says counsellors always take sides."
options.then: Karan shrugs. "Then we find one who listens to you."

options.text: "Later. I want to fix things at home first."
options.then: Karan says: "You can talk to someone while you decide."

steps.why: Talking to someone trained, with a friend beside you, makes a hard first step easier.

scenarios.relearn: A man can say 'I'm being abused and I need support' and be believed; help is for any gender.

scenarios.hook: You want a trusted person to check on you regularly while things are tense.
scenarios.setup: You call Priya to ask for a small favour.

steps.prompt: Priya answers: "Hey, what's up? You sound serious."

options.text: "Message me each evening. Call if I don't reply."
options.then: "Done," Priya says. "Starting tonight."

options.text: "Just think of me sometimes. That's enough."
options.then: Priya says: "Of course," though she isn't sure what you mean.

options.text: "It's probably not serious enough to bother you."
options.then: Priya says: "You never bother me. Tell me anyway."

options.text: "Tell everyone to check on me."
options.then: Priya says: "That's a lot of people. Let's start with me."

steps.why: A specific plan, message and follow up, gives a friend something concrete to act on.

steps.prompt: That evening Priya texts: "Checking in. All okay?"

options.text: "All okay tonight. Thanks for asking."
options.then: Priya replies: "Same time tomorrow."

options.text: "Don't worry if I miss one. I'll reply when I can."
options.then: Priya types "Okay," unsure now when a silence should worry her.

options.text: "Busy. Let's make this weekly instead."
options.then: Priya agrees, and the days in between stretch out long.

options.text: "My sister says I'm making too much of this."
options.then: Priya says: "She isn't there at night. I am, by phone."

steps.why: A plain reply keeps the check-in working, and a missed one stays a signal. None of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Priya asks: "Should we keep this up, or change something?"

options.text: "Keep it, and let's add a code word for real trouble."
options.then: Priya writes the word down. "Say it and I call."

options.text: "Let's stop. Things have been quieter lately."
options.then: Priya agrees, and the evening messages stop that week.

options.text: "Change it. If I go quiet, come to the house."
options.then: Priya says: "I'd rather call for help than walk in alone."

options.text: "My cousin says all this planning is dramatic."
options.then: Priya laughs shortly. "Planning costs us nothing."

steps.why: A code word adds a fast, quiet way to signal real trouble, on top of the daily check.

scenarios.hook: "What happens at home is private, so no one can help."
scenarios.relearn: Abuse isn't private; 'it's at home' is no shield, and help is real and reachable.

myth.un: What happens at home is private, so no one can help.
myth.re: Abuse isn't a private matter; help is real and reachable.
myth.why: 'Private' is no shield; routes like 181 and a trusted person exist exactly for harm at home.

scenarios.hook: "It only counts as abuse if it leaves a mark."

myth.un: It only counts as abuse if it leaves a mark.
myth.re: Emotional, economic and sexual abuse all count, mark or not.
myth.why: Abuse takes many forms beyond the physical, and each is real and deserves help.

scenarios.hook: "I've stayed this long, so it's too late to reach out."

myth.un: I've stayed this long, so it's too late to reach out.
myth.re: It's never too late to reach for help, whatever you've endured.
myth.why: Staying is never a reason for blame, and routes to help stay open whenever you're ready.

scenarios.hook: "No one will help unless I can prove every incident."
scenarios.relearn: You don't need proof to be believed and helped; helplines believe first.

myth.un: No one will help unless I can prove every incident.
myth.re: You don't need proof to be believed and helped.
myth.why: Helplines believe first; from the first call you deserve support, no evidence required.

myth.un: Men can't really be abused, so they can't ask for help.
myth.re: Anyone of any gender can be abused and can ask for help.
myth.why: The pattern, not the gender, defines abuse; male and other survivors are believed equally.

scenarios.hook: "Once you decide to leave, the danger is behind you."
scenarios.relearn: Risk can rise around leaving, so a careful plan matters at the riskiest time.

myth.un: Once you decide to leave, the danger is behind you.
myth.re: Risk can rise around leaving, so a careful plan matters.
myth.why: The time of leaving can be the most dangerous; a quiet safety plan helps you through it.

scenarios.hook: "With no money of my own, there's no help I can reach."
scenarios.relearn: Free, discreet routes (181, a trusted person, NALSA legal aid) reach you whatever your money.

myth.un: With no money of my own, there's no help I can reach.
myth.re: Free, discreet routes reach you whatever your money.
myth.why: 181, a trusted person and NALSA legal aid cost nothing; help isn't only for those with money.

scenarios.hook: "To really help, you should take charge and fix it for them."
scenarios.relearn: The best help asks what they need and follows their pace, never taking over.

myth.un: To really help, you should take charge and fix it for them.
myth.re: The best help asks what they need and follows their pace.
myth.why: A survivor is the expert on their own danger; taking over removes the control that keeps them safe.

scenarios.relearn: Names, threats and silent treatment used to wound are emotional abuse.
scenarios.hook: "Words can't be abuse; he never raised a hand."

myth.un: Words can't be abuse; only hands can.
myth.re: Names, threats and the silent treatment used to wound are emotional abuse.
myth.why: Fear and shame can be inflicted without a single touch.

scenarios.relearn: An 'allowance' that you must beg for, with no account of your own, is economic abuse.
scenarios.hook: "He gives me an allowance, so I have nothing to complain about."

myth.un: An allowance means he's being generous, not controlling.
myth.re: An 'allowance' you must beg for, with no account of your own, is economic abuse.
myth.why: Money handed out to keep you dependent is a leash, not a gift.

scenarios.relearn: Cutting you off from family and friends is isolation, a core tactic of coercive control.
scenarios.hook: "He keeps me from my friends because he wants me all to himself."

myth.un: Wanting you all to himself is romantic, not controlling.
myth.re: Cutting you off from family and friends is isolation, a tactic of coercive control.
myth.why: An abuser isolates so no one is left to notice or help.

scenarios.relearn: Coercive control is a pattern; many small controlling acts add up to real abuse.
scenarios.hook: "Each thing on its own is small, so none of it can be abuse."

myth.un: Each act is small, so together they can't be abuse.
myth.re: Coercive control is a pattern; small controlling acts add up to real abuse.
myth.why: It's the steady pattern, not any one act, that traps a person.

scenarios.relearn: Anyone of any gender can be a victim of abuse; the pattern, not the gender, defines it.
scenarios.hook: "A man can't really be abused by his wife."

myth.un: A man can't really be a victim of abuse.
myth.re: Anyone of any gender can be a victim; the pattern, not the gender, defines abuse.
myth.why: Control and harm don't check who they happen to.

scenarios.relearn: Abuse is the abuser's choice; nothing the other person did causes it.
scenarios.hook: "If I hadn't argued back, he wouldn't have lashed out, so it's partly mine."

myth.un: If you provoke them, the abuse is partly your doing.
myth.re: Abuse is the abuser's choice; nothing you did causes it.
myth.why: An argument is never a licence to harm someone.

scenarios.relearn: Threats to hurt you, the children, or himself to control you are abuse, not just anger.
scenarios.hook: "He only threatens; he hasn't actually done anything."

myth.un: A threat isn't abuse unless he acts on it.
myth.re: Threats to hurt you, the children, or himself to control you are abuse.
myth.why: Living under threat is itself a way of being controlled by fear.

scenarios.relearn: Jealousy used to question, check and restrict you is control, not a measure of love.
scenarios.hook: "His jealousy just shows how much he cares about me."

myth.un: Jealousy is a sign of how much he cares.
myth.re: Jealousy used to question, check and restrict you is control, not love.
myth.why: Trust expands your world; jealousy shrinks it.

scenarios.relearn: Pressuring or forcing sex when you've said no is sexual abuse, even in a marriage.
scenarios.hook: "Once you're married, refusing sex isn't really a refusal."

myth.un: A no in marriage doesn't really count as a no.
myth.re: Pressuring or forcing sex after you've said no is sexual abuse, even in marriage.
myth.why: Marriage never turns a no into a yes.

scenarios.relearn: Reading your phone and tracking your location without consent is surveillance, a form of abuse.
scenarios.hook: "He checks my phone and location just to keep me safe."

myth.un: Checking your phone and location is just keeping you safe.
myth.re: Reading your phone and tracking your location without consent is surveillance abuse.
myth.why: Safety doesn't require erasing your privacy.

scenarios.relearn: Abuse isn't a private family matter; the law and helplines exist precisely for it.
scenarios.hook: "This is a family matter; the law has no place inside a home."

myth.un: The law has no place in what happens inside a home.
myth.re: Abuse isn't a private family matter; the law and helplines exist for it.
myth.why: A closed door must never become cover for harm.

scenarios.relearn: Constantly managing someone's mood to avoid an outburst is a sign of abuse, not a happy home.
scenarios.hook: "Tiptoeing around his moods is just part of married life."

myth.un: Walking on eggshells is just normal married life.
myth.re: Constantly managing someone's mood to avoid an outburst is a sign of abuse.
myth.why: A safe home doesn't require you to disappear.

scenarios.relearn: Repeatedly twisting events so you doubt your own memory is a real abuse tactic, not your confusion.
scenarios.hook: "Maybe I really am too forgetful and dramatic, like he says."

myth.un: If he says you misremember, you're probably just confused.
myth.re: Repeatedly twisting events so you doubt your own memory is an abuse tactic.
myth.why: Making you distrust your own mind is a way to control it.

scenarios.relearn: If the cycle of harm and apology keeps repeating, the apology is part of the control, not a cure.
scenarios.hook: "He always says sorry afterwards, so it can't really be abuse."

myth.un: A heartfelt sorry afterwards means it isn't abuse.
myth.re: If harm and apology keep repeating, the apology is part of the control.
myth.why: Change is shown by it stopping, not by saying sorry again.

scenarios.relearn: Sudden gifts and sweetness right after a hurtful spell can be part of a control cycle, not proof of love.
scenarios.hook: "After every bad patch he showers me with love, so deep down he's good."

myth.un: Showering you with love after a bad patch proves he's good.
myth.re: Sudden gifts and sweetness after a hurtful spell can be part of a control cycle.
myth.why: Warmth that comes and goes on his terms is still control.

scenarios.relearn: Stopping you from working, studying or earning is economic abuse, not him 'providing'.
scenarios.hook: "He won't let me work because a good husband provides everything."

myth.un: Stopping you from working just means he provides for you.
myth.re: Stopping you from working, studying or earning is economic abuse.
myth.why: Keeping you without your own money keeps you without options.

scenarios.relearn: Naming what's happening as control, not a 'strong personality', is the first protection, not disloyalty.
scenarios.hook: "He's not abusive, he just has a strong personality."

myth.un: Calling it control is unfair; he just has a strong personality.
myth.re: Naming it as control, not a 'strong personality', is the first protection.
myth.why: A strong person lifts you up; control presses you down.

scenarios.relearn: Living amid control and fear harms children too; their safety counts, and help exists for the whole family.
scenarios.hook: "I should bear anything so the children keep their father."

myth.un: You must endure anything to keep the family together for the kids.
myth.re: Living amid control and fear harms children too; their safety counts.
myth.why: Children learn safety from a calm home, not a fearful one.

scenarios.relearn: Kind spells between controlling ones don't undo the abuse; the pattern is what defines it.
scenarios.hook: "He's so loving most days that the bad days don't really count."

myth.un: The loving days outnumber the bad ones, so it isn't abuse.
myth.re: Kind spells between controlling ones don't undo the abuse; the pattern defines it.
myth.why: An abuser is rarely cruel every hour; that's how the pattern hides.

scenarios.relearn: Needing permission to leave the house, see people or spend a rupee is coercive control.
scenarios.hook: "Asking him before I do anything is just being a respectful wife."

myth.un: Asking permission for everything is just being respectful.
myth.re: Needing permission to leave, see people or spend a rupee is coercive control.
myth.why: Respect is mutual; permission for everything is a cage.

scenarios.relearn: A partner going quiet, withdrawn or watchful can be coping with control, not contentment.

myth.un: She's quiet and stays in, so she must be content.
myth.re: A partner gone quiet, withdrawn or watchful can be coping with control.
myth.why: Sometimes silence is fear wearing the mask of calm.

scenarios.hook: Your husband has slowly taken over every money decision in the house.

steps.prompt: He tells you the joint account is closing and hands you a weekly amount. What do you do?

options.text: Name it to yourself as economic abuse
options.then: Naming it clearly, you stop second-guessing what you are seeing.

options.text: Decide the money is his, since he earns it
options.then: The rule sounds fair in your head, and the account closes on Friday.

options.text: Decide you are careless with money anyway
options.then: You hand it over believing the fault is yours, and the doubt grows.

options.text: Ask his brother whether this is usual
options.then: He says most homes run this way, and the question closes there.

steps.why: Naming a forced allowance as economic abuse, not 'his way', is how you see the pattern clearly.

steps.prompt: A week in, the allowance barely covers the groceries. What do you do?

options.text: Keep a written note of what you spend and need
options.then: The record makes the shortfall hard to argue away later.

options.text: Decide you must be shopping carelessly
options.then: You cut the list twice, and the money still runs out by Thursday.

options.text: Ask his mother to raise it with him
options.then: She says it is not her place, and tells you to manage somehow.

options.text: Tell yourself a wife shouldn't count his money
options.then: The thought quiets you, and the same gap repeats next week.

steps.why: A written record of what is actually needed builds something you can point to later.

steps.prompt: A friend quietly asks whether you have money that is really your own. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her honestly, and ask about calling 181
options.then: She helps you memorise 181, and offers her phone for the call.

options.text: Say things are fine, to protect his name
options.then: She lets it go, and the whole arrangement stays yours to carry.

options.text: Say you would have money if you managed better
options.then: She looks doubtful, and the conversation drifts somewhere else.

options.text: Say you will sort it out once things calm
options.then: The calm never quite arrives, and nothing gets sorted.

steps.why: Telling a trusted friend, and asking about a real route like 181, turns naming it into a step.

steps.prompt: Your sister offers to keep a little money for you at her house. What do you do?

options.text: Accept, and note down what she is holding
options.then: She puts it in a steel box, and you both write the amount down.

options.text: Refuse, since a wife shouldn't hide anything
options.then: The offer passes, and the week runs on his allowance again.

options.text: Say you will accept once he agrees to it
options.then: You raise it with no one, and the offer quietly lapses.

options.text: Ask her to get your parents to call him
options.then: She hesitates, worried a call from them could make things harder for you at home.

steps.why: A small amount of your own, held safely by someone you trust, is footing, not disloyalty.

scenarios.debrief: Naming a forced allowance as economic abuse is how you see the pattern; the control is his doing, never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Naming it as economic abuse, not 'his way', is the first step.

scenarios.hook: The control at home is wearing you down, and you wonder if anyone could even help.

steps.prompt: You are lying awake after another evening of his rules. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly ask a trusted person or 181 about options
options.then: You open a safe route at your own pace, without announcing it.

options.text: Decide it is private and nobody else's business
options.then: The night passes with the thought kept entirely to yourself.

options.text: Decide it only counts once it gets much worse
options.then: The line for worse moves again, and nothing changes meanwhile.

options.text: Hint at it to a relative who never asks twice
options.then: The hint passes unnoticed, and the question stays unanswered.

steps.why: Reaching a trusted person or 181 quietly keeps you safe while you learn your options.

steps.prompt: A week later, your cousin Sadia sits with you and asks how things are. What do you do?

options.text: Describe it plainly, without shrinking it
options.then: Hearing it named plainly, she takes it seriously and stays with you.

options.text: Say it will ease once you learn to please him
options.then: Sadia looks unsure, and the talk turns to what you could change, not him.

options.text: Say you have probably imagined half of it
options.then: She doesn't look convinced, and the weight of the week stays with you.

options.text: Say a wife shouldn't discuss her husband
options.then: She lets it drop for now, but says she can see something is wrong.

steps.why: Describing it plainly, without shrinking it, lets someone understand how to help you.

steps.prompt: Before leaving, Sadia says she worries about you, and asks what you would want from her. What do you do?

options.text: Say you want to go slow and stay quiet for now
options.then: She agrees, and promises to stay reachable whenever you are ready.

options.text: Ask her to decide the next steps for you
options.then: She hesitates, unsure that this is her choice to make.

options.text: Ask her to tell your whole family today
options.then: She pauses, worried that could reach him before you are ready.

options.text: Say you will decide when his mood improves
options.then: His moods come and go, and the decision stays untouched.

steps.why: Naming your own pace keeps the choice, and the safety, with you. None of this is your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Reaching a trusted person or 181 quietly keeps you safe while you learn your options, no big steps forced.
scenarios.relearn: Reaching a trusted person or 181 quietly is a safe first step.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Anjali has been telling you a little more each week about her husband.

steps.prompt: She says he checks where she is all day and decides who she may see. What do you do?

options.text: Believe her, and say none of it is her fault
options.then: She exhales, relieved nobody asked her to prove it first.

options.text: Tell her exactly what she must do now
options.then: She nods along, and says less about it the next time you meet.

options.text: Ask what she might have done to set him off
options.then: She straightens her dupatta and moves the talk to something else.

options.text: Offer to speak to him yourself this week
options.then: She looks alarmed. "Please don't. It will land back on me."

steps.why: Believing her, and saying it isn't her fault, is the support that lets her keep talking.

steps.prompt: A week later she says she isn't ready to leave or tell her family. What do you do?

options.text: Respect her pace, and ask what she needs
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "Just keep checking on me. Thank you for not pushing."

options.text: Keep gently suggesting that she leave
options.then: She changes the subject, and her replies get shorter that week.

options.text: Tell her family yourself, for her own good
options.then: Her mother calls her that night, and she is left explaining everything.

options.text: Say you can only help once she acts
options.then: She says she understands, and asks about your week instead.

steps.why: Whether and when to leave is her choice; asking what she needs keeps her trusting you.

steps.prompt: At the market she quietly asks where she could learn her options. What do you do?

options.text: Share 181 and offer to sit with her
options.then: She calls from your kitchen, with you beside her, and it feels lighter.

options.text: Tell her to look it up herself first
options.then: She says she will, and weeks pass with the idea untouched.

options.text: Call 181 for her without asking first
options.then: She looks startled that the call was made without her.

options.text: Say you will find out and get back to her
options.then: Days pass, and the quiet moment to look slips by.

steps.why: Offering the route and your company, without taking over, keeps her in charge.

scenarios.debrief: Believing her, saying it is not her fault, asking what she needs and not taking over respects her pace and keeps her safe.
scenarios.relearn: Believe her, ask what she needs, and don't take over her choices.

scenarios.hook: Your husband has started telling you that things you clearly remember never happened.

steps.prompt: He says last week's argument never happened and you imagined it. What do you do?

options.text: Trust your memory and note it down quietly
options.then: Writing it down, you steady yourself against the doubt.

options.text: Decide your memory must be unreliable
options.then: You start checking yourself before saying anything at all.

options.text: Ask a mutual friend to settle who is right
options.then: She wasn't there, and the question goes nowhere.

options.text: Tell yourself this is how all couples argue
options.then: The thought calms you, and the same denial arrives on Sunday.

steps.why: Trusting your own memory, and writing it down, resists gaslighting, a real control tactic.

steps.prompt: Days later he denies a second thing you both clearly said. What do you do?

options.text: Write down what was said, with today's date
options.then: The dated line makes the pattern harder to explain away.

options.text: Decide two people never recall it the same
options.then: The idea takes hold, and his version stands by default.

options.text: Ask him to repeat it in front of his brother
options.then: His brother laughs it off, and the subject is dropped.

options.text: Tell yourself you have been forgetful lately
options.then: You start apologising for things you are not sure you did.

steps.why: A dated record of your own turns a pattern of denial into something you can point to.

steps.prompt: Over tea, your friend Ritu asks why you seem so unsettled lately. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her plainly what has been happening
options.then: She says she believes you, and that the confusion isn't your doing.

options.text: Say your memory has simply got worse
options.then: She accepts it, and you leave carrying the same fog.

options.text: Ask her to check the story with him
options.then: She mentions it lightly to him, and he repeats his version.

options.text: Say couples shouldn't discuss their arguments
options.then: She lets it go, and the subject stays inside the house.

steps.why: Telling one person who believes you breaks the fog, and none of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: He says your family will think you are unwell if you keep this up. What do you do?

options.text: Note this down, and keep it out of his reach
options.then: You fold the page away where he never looks, and it stays yours.

options.text: Decide he may be right about how you sound
options.then: You say less at home, and his version fills the silence.

options.text: Decide that keeping any record is disloyal
options.then: Writing anything starts to feel wrong, and the weeks blur.

options.text: Ask his mother to tell him to stop saying it
options.then: She says he is only stressed, and nothing changes at home.

steps.why: A record kept somewhere safe protects your own grip on what is real.

scenarios.debrief: Trusting your memory, noting what happened and telling someone you trust resists gaslighting, a real control tactic.
scenarios.relearn: Trust your own memory; quietly note what really happened.

scenarios.hook: Whenever a disagreement gets serious, your husband brings up hurting himself.

steps.prompt: He says that if you ever leave him, he will hurt himself. What do you do?

options.text: See it as control and reach out for support
options.then: Naming it as control, you call a friend, and the blame starts to lift.

options.text: Decide that loving him means carrying this
options.then: The weight settles on you, and the words come again on Sunday.

options.text: Tell yourself he only says it when upset
options.then: You explain it away, and the threat waits for the next argument.

options.text: Ask his closest friend to talk him round
options.then: His friend says he is just emotional, and nothing shifts.

steps.why: Seeing a threat as control, not love, lets you reach support instead of carrying blame.

steps.prompt: A relative says you should never upset him, given how he gets. What do you do?

options.text: Say his reaction isn't yours to manage
options.then: The relative pauses, not used to hearing it put that way.

options.text: Decide a wife should manage his moods
options.then: The job settles quietly onto you, and the week gets heavier.

options.text: Ask her what you do that sets him off
options.then: She lists small things, and you start watching yourself all day.

options.text: Ask her to keep this between you two
options.then: She agrees, and nobody else hears what is said at home.

steps.why: His reactions are his to manage, not yours; saying so keeps responsibility where it belongs.

steps.prompt: He threatens it again after a small disagreement. What do you do?

options.text: Note it down and reach a trusted person or 181
options.then: You get a calmer, informed read from someone trained to help.

options.text: Decide the threat shows how much he loves you
options.then: The thought sits oddly with you, and the fear stays anyway.

options.text: Keep the threats secret, so no one thinks less of him
options.then: The secret sits with you alone, and the fear grows heavier.

options.text: Ask his mother to stay with you a while
options.then: She comes for a week, and the threats start again the day she leaves.

steps.why: A trusted person or 181 helps you plan safely. If he seems in real danger, call 112; his choices aren't your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later, your sister asks what has been weighing on you. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her what he says when you disagree
options.then: She takes it seriously, and says his words are not yours to carry.

options.text: Say it is nothing she needs to worry about
options.then: She lets it go, and the subject closes for another month.

options.text: Say you probably make him feel insecure
options.then: She looks unsure, and the talk turns to something lighter.

options.text: Ask if all husbands say things like this
options.then: She says some men do, and the question dissolves into gossip.

steps.why: Saying plainly what he does lets support reach you, and his threats are never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Seeing the threat as control, not love, lets you reach support instead of carrying blame that isn't yours.
scenarios.relearn: A threat to self-harm used to keep you is control, not your fault.

scenarios.hook: Your brother Vikram has been hinting at how his wife treats him at home.

steps.prompt: He says she screams at him and tracks his phone, then adds men can't be victims. What do you do?

options.text: Believe him, and say it is not his fault
options.then: He looks relieved that nobody laughed or asked him to prove it.

options.text: Tell him to be firmer with her
options.then: He tries being firmer, and the tracking carries on as before.

options.text: Say every marriage has a rough patch
options.then: He nods, and the word he almost used stays unsaid.

options.text: Ask what he does that sets her off
options.then: He starts listing his own faults, and leaves soon after.

steps.why: Believing him, and saying it isn't his fault, is what lets a man say the rest.

steps.prompt: A few days later he phones you, embarrassed to use the word abuse about himself. What do you do?

options.text: Say the word plainly, so he need not
options.then: Hearing you name it, he finally lets himself agree.

options.text: Change the subject to spare his embarrassment
options.then: He sounds relieved, and the talk drifts to his work instead.

options.text: Say most men wouldn't call it that either
options.then: He takes the excuse, and the subject cools off again.

options.text: Ask him to be sure before he says it
options.then: He second-guesses himself, and says less than he meant to.

steps.why: Naming it plainly yourself makes it easier for him to accept what is happening.

steps.prompt: Later that week he asks what help there even is for a man like him. What do you do?

options.text: Name a counsellor, and 112 if it turns dangerous
options.then: He saves both, relieved something real applies to him too.

options.text: Say there is probably nothing for men
options.then: He stops looking, and things at home stay exactly as they are.

options.text: Tell him to handle it inside the marriage
options.then: He agrees to try, and the calls between you get shorter.

options.text: Say he should wait until it gets worse
options.then: The waiting goes on, and nothing at home gets easier.

steps.why: A counsellor, a trusted person, and 112 in danger are real routes for anyone, of any gender.

scenarios.debrief: Believing him equally, saying it isn't his fault and naming real routes reminds him abuse isn't defined by gender.
scenarios.relearn: Anyone of any gender can be a victim; believe him and point to help.

Your husband has decided he should handle all the money from now on.
scenarios.setup: He brings it up over dinner, as if it is settled.

steps.prompt: He says: "Close your account. There's no need for two."

options.text: "I'll keep my own account. We can still plan together."
options.then: He frowns. "Why would you need it if I'm handling things?"

options.text: "I suppose a wife doesn't really need one."
options.then: He nods. "Good. We'll go to the bank on Saturday."

options.text: "You're right. I've always been hopeless with money."
options.then: He laughs. "At least you know it. Saturday, then."

options.text: "My mother says never to argue about money."
options.then: He says: "Your mother has sense. Saturday, then."

steps.why: Keeping your own account while offering to plan together names your need without shutting down talk.

steps.prompt: The next evening he asks: "You've gone quiet. Don't you trust me with this?"

options.text: "It's about both of us having a say, not trust."
options.then: He is quiet for a moment. "We'll see," he says, and turns on the TV.

options.text: "Trusting you means handing it all over, then."
options.then: He says: "That is what a marriage is."

options.text: "Sorry. I shouldn't have made it a big thing."
options.then: He pats your hand. "Forget it, then."

options.text: "Ask my mother. She will say the same as you."
options.then: He says: "Then it is settled, isn't it?"

steps.why: Naming it as a say for both of you, not a question of trust, keeps the real issue clear.

steps.prompt: Your cousin Farah calls and asks: "You sound tired. Is it something at home?"

options.text: "He wants my account shut. Can you help me see options?"
options.then: Farah says: "We'll look together. 181 can talk you through your options."

options.text: "Nothing worth telling. It stays between us two."
options.then: Farah drops it, and the subject stays inside your house.

options.text: "He says it is all one pot now. That is normal, no?"
options.then: Farah hesitates. "Normal isn't the same as fair."

options.text: "Talk to him for me. He listens to you."
options.then: Farah says: "That would land back on you, not me."

steps.why: Asking someone you trust about your options keeps a footing of your own. This is not your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Naming your need for your own footing, calmly, is the assertive line.

scenarios.hook: You said no to sex tonight, and your husband won't let it go.
scenarios.setup: He follows you into the room, still talking.

steps.prompt: He says: "You know it's your duty as my wife."

options.text: "I said no, and that stands. It is not a duty."
options.then: He goes quiet, surprised you held your ground.

options.text: "Maybe marriage does mean I can't refuse."
options.then: He says: "Good that you know it," and keeps pressing his point.

options.text: "Sorry. I know I am being difficult tonight."
options.then: He says: "At least you can see that."

options.text: "My aunt says a wife never says no."
options.then: He says: "Your aunt understands marriage."

steps.why: Holding your no plainly, without owing a reason, keeps consent yours inside a marriage.

steps.prompt: The next day your friend Neha asks: "You're quiet. Is something wrong at home?"

options.text: "He keeps pushing for sex when I have said no."
options.then: Neha sits down beside you. "That is not something you have to take."

options.text: "Nothing. Husbands are like that everywhere."
options.then: Neha lets it go, then says: "I'm here if that changes."

options.text: "It is my fault. I refuse too often."
options.then: Neha frowns. "Refusing is not something you apologise for."

options.text: "It is private. Wives don't discuss such things."
options.then: Neha nods slowly. "The offer to listen stands, whenever."

steps.why: None of this is your fault, and telling one person you trust takes it out of the house.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Neha asks: "I keep thinking about you. Would talking to someone trained help?"

options.text: "Yes. Sit with me while I call 181 tomorrow."
options.then: Neha says: "I'll be there at eleven, when the house is empty."

options.text: "No. This is between a husband and a wife."
options.then: Neha says: "Even in a marriage, you can ask for help."

options.text: "My mother says helplines break up homes."
options.then: Neha shakes her head. "A phone call breaks nothing."

options.text: "Ask his sister to speak to him instead."
options.then: Neha hesitates. "That could come straight back on you."

steps.why: A trained voice on 181, with a friend beside you, is support, not a step you cannot undo.

scenarios.relearn: Holding your no, kindly and clearly, is the assertive line.

scenarios.hook: Lately your husband wants more say over how you spend your days.
scenarios.setup: He says it flatly, like a new house rule.

steps.prompt: He says: "From now on, ask me before you go out."

options.text: "I'll tell you my plans. I don't need permission."
options.then: He frowns. "Isn't that the same thing?"

options.text: "Maybe that is what respect looks like."
options.then: He nods. "Finally, some sense."

options.text: "Sorry. I should have thought of that myself."
options.then: He says: "As long as you know now."

options.text: "My bhabhi says good wives always ask."
options.then: He says: "Then it is settled."

steps.why: Offering to share plans, without asking permission, keeps him informed without control.

steps.prompt: Later he says: "I just feel better knowing where my wife is at all times."

options.text: "Telling you is respect. Asking is permission."
options.then: He goes quiet, turning the difference over.

options.text: "Maybe a husband should always know."
options.then: He says: "Good. Simple."

options.text: "Sorry. I never meant to make you worry."
options.then: He says: "Then ask first, and I won't."

options.text: "Only if you check with me as well."
options.then: He laughs. "Why would I need to?"

steps.why: Naming the difference between telling and asking keeps the boundary clear, not blurred.

steps.prompt: Your sister calls and asks: "You sound careful lately. What's going on?"

options.text: "He wants me to ask before I go out anywhere."
options.then: She says: "That is not nothing. Tell me when it happens again."

options.text: "Nothing. Every house has its own rules."
options.then: She lets it go, and the call turns to her new job.

options.text: "He only worries about me. I am out too much."
options.then: She hesitates. "Worry doesn't need a rule book."

options.text: "Don't ask. You will only make it worse."
options.then: She says: "Alright. I am at the end of the phone."

steps.why: Telling one person outside the house keeps a controlling rule visible, and it is not your fault.

steps.prompt: His mother says: "A good wife always checks with her husband first."

options.text: "I keep him informed. That is different."
options.then: She looks unconvinced, and says nothing more about it.

options.text: "Perhaps that is what a good wife is."
options.then: She smiles. "Now you understand."

options.text: "Checking first keeps the peace, I suppose."
options.then: She nods. "That is how this house has always run."

options.text: "My own mother never asked anyone."
options.then: She says: "Every house is different, beta."

steps.why: Naming the difference, informed versus permitted, holds your boundary under family pressure.

scenarios.relearn: Declining to live under a permission rule is the assertive line.

scenarios.hook: Your husband keeps rewriting what happened between you, calmly and often.
scenarios.setup: Tonight it is last week's argument.

steps.prompt: He says: "That argument never happened. You imagined it."

options.text: "It did happen, and I trust what I remember."
options.then: He shrugs, says "If you say so," and turns the television on.

options.text: "Maybe I did imagine the whole thing."
options.then: He says: "You do that a lot lately."

options.text: "Sorry. I have been muddled this week."
options.then: He says: "Rest more. You will feel better."

options.text: "Your mother says I get confused easily."
options.then: He says: "So she has noticed it too."

steps.why: Saying plainly that you trust your memory holds your own reality against the denial.

steps.prompt: The next evening he says: "You always exaggerate. Everyone says so."

options.text: "I am not exaggerating. That is what I remember."
options.then: He looks away and says nothing for a while.

options.text: "Maybe everyone is right about me after all."

options.text: Decide a wife shouldn't earn on the side

steps.why: None of this is your fault, and a route like 181 stays open however the family talks.

scenarios.debrief: No money of your own is control, not a dead end; 181 can help.
scenarios.relearn: With no money of your own, 181 can explain maintenance and quiet first steps.

scenarios.hook: His anger tonight has turned into something you have not seen before.

options.text: Get to a safer spot and call 112

options.text: Decide 112 is only for strangers, not family
options.then: The number goes undialled while the shouting goes on.

options.text: Decide you must have caused this tonight
options.then: You search yourself for the fault, and the fear stays.

options.text: Decide it only counts as danger once he hits you
options.then: The phone stays unused in your hand as the shouting comes closer.

steps.why: Your safety comes before anything else, and 112 is the number that sends help right now.

steps.prompt: Next morning the house is quiet, and your hands are still shaking. What do you do?

options.text: Call 181 and ask what to do if it happens again
options.then: The counsellor helps you plan where to go and who to call.

options.text: Decide it won't happen again, and put it away
options.then: The morning passes, and no plan ever gets made.

options.text: Decide it happened because you answered back

options.text: Ask his brother to warn him off it

steps.why: A plan made in a calm hour, with 181, is what you can use in a frightening one.

steps.prompt: A relative says you should have just calmed him down. What do you do?

options.text: Say calming his anger was never your job

options.text: Decide you should have managed his mood

options.text: Promise her you'll keep it within the family
options.then: She seems relieved, and you feel more alone with it than before.

options.text: Ask her what she would have done instead
options.then: She lists things she has never had to try, and you feel worse.

steps.why: Calming his anger was never your job, and nothing you did makes his violence your fault.

scenarios.debrief: In immediate danger, your safety comes first: get to a safer spot and call 112.
scenarios.relearn: In immediate danger, get to safety and call 112.

scenarios.hook: A survivor has come to you for help, and you don't want to take over.

options.then: They let out a breath, and start with what worries them most.

options.text: Make the calls and decisions for them
options.then: You start listing calls to make, and they fall silent in their chair.

options.text: Ask them to go through every detail first
options.then: They start from the beginning, and tire before reaching what they need.

options.text: Tell them what most survivors do here
options.then: They measure themselves against people they have never met.

steps.why: Good help asks what they need and says it is not their fault, from the first question.

steps.prompt: They say they need time to think before deciding anything. What do you do?

options.text: Give them that time, with no deadline
options.then: They come back the next week with a question of their own.

options.text: Set a gentle deadline to keep things moving
options.then: They start apologising for how long they are taking.

options.text: Tell them waiting only makes it worse
options.then: They leave carrying a new worry about every week they take.

options.text: Check in every single day until they decide
options.then: The daily calls start to feel like a clock ticking.

steps.prompt: At a later session, they ask what to do if it turns dangerous again at home. What do you do?

options.text: Name 112 for danger and 181 for options
options.then: They learn both numbers by heart before they leave.

options.text: Say you will come over there yourself
options.then: They call you first, and the minutes stretch while you travel.

options.text: Tell them to avoid upsetting him for now
options.then: They take on the job of managing his temper again.

options.text: Say it really depends on what happens
options.then: They leave with nothing specific to hold on to.

steps.why: Naming 112 for danger and 181 for options gives them something usable, not just comfort.

steps.prompt: Months later they say they worry they have been too slow. What do you say?

options.text: Say there is no right speed, only theirs
options.then: They nod, and some of the worry leaves their face.

options.text: Say you had hoped they would go faster

options.text: Say now is the time to speed things up

options.text: Move the talk on to what comes next

steps.why: The pace was always theirs to set, and saying so lifts a worry that was never theirs to carry.

scenarios.debrief: Good help asks, follows the survivor's lead, names real routes, and never puts the blame on them.
scenarios.relearn: Support a survivor by asking what they need and following their lead.

scenarios.hook: Your colleague Sameer has started hinting at how things are with his wife at home.

options.text: Laugh along, so he doesn't feel embarrassed

options.text: Say there is probably nothing for men

scenarios.debrief: The pattern, not gender, defines abuse; believe him, and remember it is never his fault.

scenarios.hook: Things at home keep getting tenser, and you want to be quietly ready, just in case.

options.text: Decide he would never really hurt you

options.text: Decide it won't get worse, so why prepare

options.text: Ring your aunt to ask if you're overreacting

options.text: Get copies to a trusted friend's house

options.text: Snap photos of them on the shared phone

options.text: Ask his sister to keep them safe for you

options.text: Ask several relatives to be your contact too

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a thought nags that planning ahead makes you the disloyal one. What do you do?

scenarios.debrief: Quiet planning builds readiness without raising risk, and needing it is never your fault.

scenarios.hook: A friend just disclosed abuse. Spot the two responses that BLAME her.

"It's not your fault"

scenarios.hook: Spot the two WRONG statements about getting help.

scene.text: 112 is for an emergency

scenarios.why: Help isn't only for physical harm, and helplines won't report back to him; both lines are false.

"It's only abuse if he hits me"

Calling the police without asking her
"I'll go at your pace"

"I believe you"

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that dress up control as love.

"I check your phone because I love you"

"What happens at home is no one's business"
"You're allowed to reach out"
"It's our marriage, so no one can help"

scenarios.hook: You've decided to call the Women Helpline 181 for the first time.
scenarios.setup: The line connects, and a calm voice answers.

steps.prompt: The counsellor says: "Hello, 181. How can I help you today?"

options.text: "I need to talk about what's happening at home."
options.then: "Of course," she says gently. "Take your time. I'm listening."

options.text: "Sorry to bother you. It's probably nothing."
options.then: She says: "You're not bothering me. Please go on."

options.text: "I shouldn't take a line someone else needs."
options.then: She says softly: "This line is for you too. I'm here."

options.text: "My family would say I'm making a fuss."
options.then: She says: "What matters here is what you are going through."

steps.why: Saying plainly that you need to talk lets the counsellor actually help you.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Can you tell me a bit about what's been happening?"

options.text: "He controls all the money, and it's worse now."
options.then: "I hear you," she says. "Controlling money is economic abuse."

options.text: "Maybe it's my fault. I make him angry."
options.then: She says gently: "Nothing you do makes his behaviour your fault."

options.text: "I don't want to get him into any trouble."
options.then: She says: "This call is about you being safe, not about trouble."

options.text: "Every marriage has problems like this."
options.then: She says gently: "Even so, you deserve to know where you stand."

steps.why: Naming what's actually happening lets her name the pattern. None of it is your fault.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Would it help to hear what options you have?"

options.text: "Yes, please. I'd like to know my options."
options.then: She goes through them slowly, checking what you understood.

options.text: "Just tell me what I have to do."
options.then: She says gently: "I can share options. The choice stays yours."

options.text: "There's no point. Nothing will change."
options.then: She says: "Let me share them anyway. You can decide later."

options.text: "My neighbour says helplines just send police."
options.then: She says: "We can simply talk through your options first."

steps.why: Asking to understand your options, plainly, is exactly what the call is for.

scenarios.relearn: On 181 you can simply say you need to talk and ask about your options; you're not bothering anyone.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Pooja turns up at your door late one evening.
scenarios.setup: She keeps her voice low and watches your face.

steps.prompt: She says: "He hurt me again last night. I don't know what to do."

options.text: "I believe you. It's not your fault. I'm here."
options.then: She starts crying. "I thought no one would believe me."

options.text: "Are you sure you're not reading too much into it?"
options.then: She hesitates. "Maybe." Then, quietly: "No. It happened."

options.text: "What happened just before? Did something set him off?"
options.then: She stiffens. "I didn't do anything," she says.

options.text: "You should have left after the first time."
options.then: She looks away. "It isn't that easy," she says.

steps.why: Belief and no blame, said plainly, lets her keep talking to you. It is never her fault.

steps.prompt: After a moment she asks: "So what do I even do now?"

options.text: "What do you need most right now?"
options.then: She thinks. "Just for someone to know," she says.

options.text: "You need a plan, starting today."
options.then: She shakes her head. "I can't think that far yet."

options.text: "I'll tell you exactly what to do."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I suppose," she says, unsure.

options.text: "Stay with your parents until he changes."
options.then: She says: "They would send me straight back to him."

steps.why: Asking what she needs, instead of prescribing steps, keeps the choice with her.

steps.prompt: A few days later she says: "I'm scared people will find out."

options.text: "I won't tell anyone unless you want me to."
options.then: She relaxes a little. "Thank you. That helps."

options.text: "People will find out sooner or later anyway."
options.then: She pales. "That's what scares me," she says.

options.text: "Your family ought to know. I could tell them."
options.then: She grips your arm. "Please don't. Not yet."

options.text: "You shouldn't be scared of that."
options.then: She says: "Easy for you to say," and looks away.

steps.why: Respecting her control over who knows keeps the trust between you, and her safety, intact.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Is there anyone who actually helps with this?"

options.text: "181 can explain options. Shall I sit with you?"
options.then: "Yes," she says quietly. "I'd like that."

options.text: "You could look that up yourself sometime."
options.then: She nods. "Maybe," she says, and puts her phone away.

options.text: "Let me call them for you right now."
options.then: She looks startled. "Wait. I want to be the one who calls."

options.text: "I'm honestly not sure anyone can help with this."
options.then: Her face falls. "Then I'm on my own," she says.

steps.why: Naming a real route, and offering to sit with her, turns support into something she can use.

scenarios.relearn: Lead with belief and no blame: 'I believe you. It's not your fault. I'm here.'

scenarios.hook: Your husband controls every rupee in the house, and a neighbour gave you a counsellor's number.
scenarios.setup: You sit down across from her, unsure where to begin.

steps.prompt: She asks gently: "What brings you in today?"

options.text: "He controls all the money and leaves me none."
options.then: She nods slowly. "That has a name. It is economic abuse."

options.text: "It's fine. He handles money because he earns it."
options.then: She nods. "Let's start there, then."

options.text: "Maybe I spend too much. It's my own fault."
options.then: She says: "Needing money for yourself is not a fault."

options.text: "Nothing serious, really. Just money things."
options.then: She says: "Money things can be serious. Take your time."

steps.why: Naming it plainly, that he controls the money and leaves you none, is naming economic abuse.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Can you tell me how money works in your home?"

options.text: "I have to ask him for every rupee I need."
options.then: She writes it down. "Thank you. That helps me understand."

options.text: "It works fine. I don't really need money."
options.then: She says gently: "Everyone needs a little for their own small things."

options.text: "I shouldn't say. It's our private matter."
options.then: She says: "You can share only what feels okay."

options.text: "My mother says a good wife never asks for money."
options.then: She says: "Your own view matters here too."

steps.why: Describing it plainly, without shrinking it, shows the real shape of the control.

steps.prompt: She asks: "If you could have a little footing of your own, what would help?"

options.text: "Some money I control myself, even a little."
options.then: She nods. "Then let's find a small, safe way to start."

options.text: "Whatever you think is best for me."
options.then: She smiles. "This part should be your own idea."

options.text: "Nothing. A wife shouldn't want her own money."
options.then: She says: "Wanting some footing is not selfish."

options.text: "For him to change, so I don't need any."
options.then: She says: "His choices are his. Let's think about you."

steps.why: Naming a small, concrete want makes a first step reachable, and none of this is your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Naming it plainly, 'he controls all the money and leaves me none', is naming economic abuse.

scenarios.hook: Things with your husband have got harder, and you want to understand your rights.
scenarios.setup: You dial 15100 and wait for someone to pick up.

steps.prompt: A voice answers: "Legal aid helpline. How can I help?"

options.text: "I can't afford a lawyer. Can you explain my options?"
options.then: "Of course," they say. "Let's go through it together."

options.text: "I have no money, so there's no point asking, is there?"
options.then: They say: "There is every point. This service is free."

options.text: "Sorry. I'm sure you have more serious cases."
options.then: They say gently: "Your case matters too. Please go on."

options.text: "I just want a quick opinion, nothing formal."
options.then: They say: "We can do more than that, if you like."

steps.why: Naming the cost barrier plainly is exactly what free legal aid exists to remove.

steps.prompt: They ask: "Can you tell me a little about your situation?"

options.text: "He controls the money and stops me going out."
options.then: They note it down. "That can count as economic abuse."

options.text: "It's probably not serious enough for you."
options.then: They say: "Let's talk it through anyway. That's what we're for."

options.text: "It's a family matter. I shouldn't really say."
options.then: They say: "Family matters are exactly what we help with."

options.text: "I don't want him to get into trouble."
options.then: They say: "Understanding your options commits you to nothing."

steps.why: Describing it plainly helps them match you to the right help. None of it is your fault.

steps.prompt: They ask: "Shall I explain the kinds of help the law can offer?"

options.text: "Yes, please. Go slowly, so I can follow."
options.then: They explain protection orders, maintenance and residence rights, step by step.

options.text: "No need. The law only helps if he hits me."
options.then: They say: "Not only. It covers much more than that."

options.text: "Just file whatever gets results fastest."
options.then: They say: "Let's first understand what fits your situation."

options.text: "I'll ask my husband what he thinks first."
options.then: They pause. "Telling him first could make things harder for you at home."

steps.why: Asking them to explain, at a pace you can follow, turns free aid into information you can use.

scenarios.relearn: Free legal aid on 15100 is for exactly this; ask it to explain your options under the DV Act 2005.

scenarios.hook: Farida, a woman you counsel, has been describing her husband's control for weeks.
scenarios.setup: Today she sits quietly, turning her dupatta in her hands.

steps.prompt: She says: "I don't think I'm ready to do anything yet."

options.text: "That's okay. Here are routes, for when you're ready."
options.then: She memorises 181 and 112. "Only when I'm ready?" she asks.

options.text: "You have to leave him today, or I can't help."
options.then: She flinches. "Then maybe I shouldn't have come."

options.text: "If you don't act now, what happens is on you."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "So it's my fault now?"

options.text: "Take all the time you need. We can talk about help later."
options.then: She nods. "Thank you. I wouldn't know who to call anyway."

steps.why: Offering real routes while leaving the pace to her is help without pressure.

steps.prompt: She asks: "What if I never feel ready?"

options.text: "Then the door stays open, with no conditions."
options.then: She lets out a breath. "Okay. That helps."

options.text: "You will. Most people get there eventually."
options.then: She looks unsure. "And if I'm not most people?"

options.text: "Then I don't know what more I can do."
options.then: She looks down. "I've let you down, then."

options.text: "Then maybe try couples counselling with him."
options.then: She stiffens. "He would never let me speak freely there."

steps.why: Keeping the door open, with no condition attached, means help is there whenever she wants it.

steps.prompt: Weeks later she calls and asks: "If I did want help now, where would I start?"

options.text: "181 for options, and 112 if you're in danger."
options.then: She repeats them softly. "Okay. I'll remember."

options.text: "Why now? What has changed since last time?"
options.then: She hesitates. "Does it matter?" she asks quietly.

options.text: "I'm so glad you finally came around."
options.then: She pauses. "I didn't know I was late," she says.

options.text: "I'll call them for you and set it all up."
options.then: She says: "I'd rather make the call myself."

steps.why: Naming real routes plainly, with no comment on her timing, respects her pace. It is never her fault.

scenarios.relearn: Offer routes at the survivor's pace, never an ultimatum: 'whenever you're ready, here are the routes.'

scenarios.hook: Things at home feel unpredictable, and you trust your friend Asha more than anyone.
scenarios.setup: You meet her for tea, a little nervous.

steps.prompt: Asha asks: "You said you wanted to ask me something?"

options.text: "Things at home scare me. Could we agree a signal?"
options.then: Asha takes your hand. "Of course. Whatever you need."

options.text: "Never mind. I really don't want to worry you."
options.then: Asha puts her cup down. "I've seen how tense you are at home."

options.text: "My husband says I overthink everything."
options.then: Asha frowns. "You're not overthinking. I've seen how he is."

options.text: "Nothing big. Just check on me now and then."
options.then: Asha nods. "I will. I've been worried about you at home."

steps.why: Saying plainly that you're scared, and asking for a signal, gets real help in place early.

steps.prompt: Asha says: "I want a way to know if you're ever in danger. What message should we use?"

options.text: "If I text 'send the recipe', don't ring me. Call 112."
options.then: Asha repeats it back. "Recipe means 112, and no calling you."

options.text: "Let's not pick one yet. It feels like jinxing it."
options.then: Asha says: "A word costs nothing. Let's still pick one."

options.text: "Any message will do. You'll just know."
options.then: Asha looks worried. "I might miss it. Let's be exact."

options.text: "My cousin says code words are only for films."
options.then: Asha shakes her head. "Films or not, it could help."

steps.why: A clear word and one clear action, 112 without ringing you, turn a signal into help she can give.

steps.prompt: A month later Asha asks: "Do you still want a signal between us?"

options.text: "Yes. Let's settle the exact word and what you do."
options.then: Asha saves the word in her phone under a dull name. "Done."

options.text: "No. Things are calmer, so there's no need."
options.then: Asha pauses. "I'd still like one, just in case."

options.text: "Let's use a new word every week, to be safe."
options.then: Asha laughs nervously. "I'd never keep up with that."

options.text: "Yes, but let's add my whole family to it."
options.then: Asha hesitates. "The more who know, the more could reach him."

steps.why: Settling the exact word and action keeps help ready, and needing it is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: A code word with a trusted person lets you signal for help quickly, without saying it aloud.

scenarios.hook: Your wife controls who you see and mocks you in front of family, and it has worn you down.
scenarios.setup: Your elder cousin Rohit drives you home after a wedding.

steps.prompt: Rohit asks: "You looked miserable all evening. Want to talk?"

options.text: "This is hard to say. I'm being controlled at home."
options.then: Rohit pulls over. "I'm listening. Take your time."

options.text: "Nothing. Men don't really get hurt like that."
options.then: Rohit glances over. "Says who? Something is clearly wrong."

options.text: "It's my fault. I'm not a proper husband."
options.then: Rohit frowns. "That doesn't sound like you talking."

options.text: "Just tired. Weddings always drain me."
options.then: Rohit says: "I've seen you tired. This isn't it."

steps.why: Naming it, even when it is hard to say, lets someone you trust actually hear you.

steps.prompt: Rohit says quietly: "I've noticed how she talks to you. What do you need?"

options.text: "I need to talk to someone who knows about this."
options.then: Rohit nods. "Then let's find that person together."

options.text: "Nothing. I should handle it myself, like a man."
options.then: Rohit shakes his head. "Being a man doesn't mean alone."

options.text: "Don't tell anyone. They'd laugh at me."
options.then: Rohit nods. "I won't. But I'm not dropping this."

options.text: "Talk to her for me. She'll listen to you."
options.then: Rohit hesitates. "That could make it worse for you at home."

steps.why: Saying what you need, plainly, lets support reach you. None of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: Rohit asks: "So who could you actually talk to about this?"

options.text: "A counsellor. Will you help me find one?"
options.then: Rohit says: "This week. I'll sit with you when you call."

options.text: "No one would take a man's word for this."
options.then: Rohit says: "A counsellor would. And I do."

options.text: "It will stop once she's less stressed."
options.then: Rohit says quietly: "Stress doesn't explain how she treats you."

options.text: "I'll ask her parents to sort her out."
options.then: Rohit winces. "They'd take her side, and she'd hear of it."

steps.why: Reaching a counsellor, with someone beside you, turns being believed into real help.

scenarios.relearn: Anyone of any gender can be hurt; saying 'I'm being controlled and I need help' is strength, not weakness.

scenarios.hook: Your neighbour Rukhsana has been coming to you after bad nights at home.
scenarios.setup: Tonight she sits on your sofa, arms folded tight.

steps.prompt: She says: "I'm not ready to go to the police. Please don't push."

options.text: "That's your call. What would feel safe to you?"
options.then: She unfolds her arms. "Just somewhere to go on bad nights."

options.text: "I'm calling them anyway. It's for your own good."
options.then: She grabs your wrist. "Please don't. He'll know it was me."

options.text: "Then I don't know how else I can help you."
options.then: Her face falls. "Please. I have no one else."

options.text: "Okay. But you really should reconsider soon."
options.then: She tenses. "You sound like my mother."

steps.why: Respecting her no, and asking what feels safe, keeps support hers to shape. It is not her fault.

steps.prompt: She asks: "What if nothing ever feels safe enough?"

options.text: "Then we start small. You can come here anytime."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Anytime? Even late?"

options.text: "Something will have to change eventually."
options.then: She sighs. "Everyone keeps telling me that."

options.text: "Then maybe it's time you just decided."
options.then: She stiffens. "Decided what? To lose everything?"

options.text: "If you stayed calmer, he might calm down too."
options.then: She stares at you. "So it's on me to fix him?"

steps.why: Offering small, safe steps keeps support moving without forcing a choice she isn't ready for.

steps.prompt: Months later she says: "I think I'm ready to call the police myself."

options.text: "I'm here if you want company. It's your call."
options.then: She smiles a little. "Company, then. Not control."

options.text: "Finally! Give me the phone. I'll call for you."
options.then: She holds on to the phone. "No. I want to do this myself."

options.text: "About time. I was starting to really worry."
options.then: She flinches. "I came when I could," she says.

options.text: "Are you sure you're ready this time?"
options.then: She hesitates. "I was, until you asked."

steps.why: Offering company while the call stays hers keeps the choice in her hands, even now.

scenarios.relearn: Respect the survivor's choice; ask what feels safe instead of overriding them.

myth.re: Abuse can be emotional, economic, sexual or coercive control, not only physical.
myth.why: India's DV Act 2005 recognises emotional, sexual and economic abuse, not just physical harm.

scenarios.relearn: Abuse is more than physical; emotional, economic, sexual and coercive control all count.

myth.re: Withholding money to deny your independence is economic abuse, not practicality.
myth.why: Cutting off your access to money to trap or control you is a recognised form of abuse.

scenarios.relearn: Controlling money to deny your independence is economic abuse, not 'just practical'.

myth.un: "What happens between a couple is private, so no one can help."

myth.why: Abuse isn't a private family matter; routes like 181, 112 and the DV Act 2005 exist to reach in.

myth.why: Lines like 181 and 1091 are confidential and survivor-led; they help you build a safety plan, not force any action.

myth.re: Consent stays yours inside marriage; you can say no at any time.
myth.why: Marriage is not standing consent; your body remains your own and a past yes isn't a permanent yes.

scenarios.relearn: Marriage is not standing consent; you can say no any time and your body stays yours.

myth.re: Anyone of any gender can be a victim and deserves equal support.
myth.why: The pattern of control and harm, not the gender, defines abuse; silenced survivors are believed equally.

myth.un: "I've stayed this long, so it's too late to get any help."
myth.re: Staying is never a reason for blame, and a route still exists today.
myth.why: Survivors stay for many safe and complex reasons; help, through 181, 1091, 112 or a trusted person, remains.
